stem: A 4-month-old boy with down syndrome exhibits poor weight gain, tachypnea, a low-pitched grade 2 systolic murmur and a fixed splitting of S2. Chest X-ray reveals cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascularity. Electrocardiography documents biventricular hypertrophy and a superior frontal plane QRS axis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: An infant with Down syndrome, failure to thrive, tachypnea, cardiomegaly and plethoric lungs has a large left to right shunt. The fixed splitting of S2 points to an atrial level component, biventricular hypertrophy means both atrial and ventricular shunting, and a superior frontal QRS axis is the ECG hallmark of AVSD, the classic Down syndrome lesion.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coarctation gives upper limb hypertension with weak or delayed femoral pulses and is linked to Turner syndrome; it does not cause fixed split S2, plethoric lungs or a superior axis.
B. PDA gives a continuous machinery murmur with bounding pulses; S2 is not fixed split and the axis is not superior. Think PDA in prematurity or congenital rubella.
C. An isolated VSD gives a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border without fixed S2 splitting or a superior axis. It is the second most common lesion in Down syndrome.
key_concept:
Down syndrome + fixed split S2 + superior (left) QRS axis = AVSD (endocardial cushion defect).
  • Down: AVSD, then VSD
  • Turner: coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve
  • Fixed split S2: atrial level shunt (ASD or AVSD)
  • Superior axis on ECG: AVSD (also primum ASD)
  • Large shunt: cardiomegaly, plethora, early heart failure
exam_pearl: Fixed split S2 with a NORMAL or right axis suggests secundum ASD; a SUPERIOR axis in Down syndrome flips it to AVSD.

stem: In which of the following conditions would you expect a bone age greater than the chronologic age?
why_right: The question asks where bone age exceeds chronological age. In congenital adrenal hyperplasia excess adrenal androgens accelerate epiphyseal maturation, so bone age runs ahead. These children are tall early but fuse early, ending with short adult height.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypothyroidism: thyroid hormone is needed for skeletal maturation, so bone age is markedly delayed.
B. Chronic renal failure: chronic illness slows growth and delays bone age.
C. Familial short stature: bone age equals chronological age; the child is simply following short parents.
key_concept:
Sex steroid excess advances bone age; most growth failure delays it.
  • Advanced: CAH, precocious puberty, obesity, exogenous sex steroids
  • Delayed: hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, chronic illness (CKD, IBD), constitutional delay
  • Normal: familial short stature
  • CAH: commonest cause 21 hydroxylase deficiency; raised 17 hydroxyprogesterone
exam_pearl: Tall child now but short adult = advanced bone age from androgens or estrogens.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1895).

stem: Which of the following syndromes is associated with coarctation of the aorta?
why_right: Turner syndrome (45,X) is the syndrome classically linked to coarctation of the aorta, along with bicuspid aortic valve. A short girl with upper limb hypertension and weak femoral pulses should prompt karyotype for Turner.
why_wrong_block:
A. Down syndrome is associated with AVSD (endocardial cushion defect), then VSD; coarctation is not its signature lesion.
C. Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is mainly associated with VSD and PDA, with overlapping fingers and rocker bottom feet.
D. Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) is mainly associated with VSD, ASD and PDA, with midline defects such as cleft lip and palate.
key_concept:
Syndrome to heart lesion pairs:
  • Turner: coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve
  • Down: AVSD, VSD
  • Edwards (T18): VSD, PDA
  • Patau (T13): VSD, ASD, PDA
  • Williams: supravalvular aortic stenosis
  • Noonan: pulmonary valve stenosis
exam_pearl: Turner = coarctation, but Noonan (normal karyotype, similar look) = pulmonary stenosis; do not mix them up.

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with a 1-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting. He was afebrile and has no diarrhea. He has bilateral knee pain, and there was some tenderness of the knee joints, but no effusions. Within 24 hours, he developed a rash on his legs and buttocks, which is petechial and purpuric, and his platelet count was normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: rash on his legs and buttocks
why_right: A 4-year-old with abdominal pain and vomiting, bilateral knee pain without effusion, then a petechial and purpuric rash on the legs and buttocks with a normal platelet count is the classic picture of HSP (IgA vasculitis). The purpura is vasculitic, not thrombocytopenic, and GI symptoms may precede the rash.
why_wrong_block:
A. SLE is rare at age 4, usually affects adolescent girls, and tends to cause malar rash and cytopenias, not dependent purpura with normal platelets.
B. HUS follows bloody diarrhea and causes hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury; here there is no diarrhea and platelets are normal.
D. Kawasaki disease needs fever for 5 days or more with conjunctivitis, mucosal and extremity changes and lymphadenopathy; this child is afebrile.
key_concept:
HSP = purpura with normal platelets + arthralgia + abdominal pain + renal involvement.
  • Typical age: about 3 to 10 years, often after URTI
  • Rash: palpable purpura on legs and buttocks
  • Platelets and coagulation: normal
  • GI risk: intussusception
  • Follow up: urine and BP for nephritis
exam_pearl: Purpura with LOW platelets points to ITP, HUS or leukemia; purpura with NORMAL platelets on the legs and buttocks points to HSP.

stem: A 6-month-old infant with cough and fever diagnosed as bronchiolitis. On examination, she had mild distress with intercostal retraction and chest auscultation reveals diffuse crackles. Blood pressure 92/67 mmHg, Heart rate 145 /min, Respiratory rate 56 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 89 %. Which of the following is the best management?
OptA: Admit for oxygen and hydration therapy
OptB: Send home with instruction when to come back
OptC: Admit for antibiotics and oxygen administration
OptD: Admit for bronchodilation and steroid management
why_right: Bronchiolitis is viral and managed supportively. This infant has SpO2 89%, RR 56 and intercostal retractions, so she is hypoxic and needs admission for supplemental oxygen and fluid support (feeding is often impaired by tachypnea).
why_wrong_block:
B. Discharge is safe only for a well infant feeding adequately with normal saturation; hypoxia and tachypnea make it unsafe here.
C. Bronchiolitis is viral (mostly RSV); antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of secondary bacterial infection. Crackles are expected in bronchiolitis and do not mean pneumonia.
D. Bronchodilators and steroids are not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis because they do not improve outcomes; they belong to asthma management.
key_concept:
Bronchiolitis = supportive care: oxygen if hypoxic + hydration/feeding support.
  • Cause: RSV most common, under 2 years
  • Clinical diagnosis; CXR not routine
  • Admit: hypoxia, significant distress, poor feeding, apnea, very young age
  • Not routine: antibiotics, bronchodilators, steroids
exam_pearl: Same infant with normal saturation and good feeding goes home with return precautions; low saturation flips the answer to admission.

stem: IUGR neonate placed under warmer, he is still hypothermic despite warm environment, how to manage
OptC: Reassure + change environment ( increase warmer temperature i guess)
why_right: Temperature instability, especially hypothermia that persists despite a warm environment, is a classic sign of neonatal sepsis. Once environmental cause is excluded (he is already under a warmer), the neonate needs a sepsis workup (blood culture, CBC, CRP, consider LP) and prompt empirical IV antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Checking and correcting glucose is part of care in an IUGR neonate, but IV dextrose treats hypoglycemia, not the cause of refractory hypothermia; it is right when the glucose is documented low.
C. Simply turning up the warmer and reassuring ignores the warning sign; adjusting the environment is right only when the baby is cold because of an inadequate thermal environment.
D. Skin-to-skin contact is a good first measure for routine thermal care of a stable newborn, but it does not address hypothermia that persists despite active warming.
key_concept:
Persistent neonatal hypothermia despite adequate warming = suspect sepsis until proven otherwise.
  • Neonatal sepsis signs are nonspecific: temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, apnea, hypoglycemia
  • Neonates (especially preterm/IUGR) often get hypothermia rather than fever with infection
  • Workup: blood culture, CBC, CRP, consider LP
  • Start empirical IV antibiotics without waiting for results
exam_pearl: First fix the environment; if the baby stays cold despite a warmer, the problem is the baby, so think sepsis.

stem: 10 years old sudden loss of consciousness then regained while running. all physical examination normal except ejection systolic murmur. What Is the most appropriate test?
why_right: Syncope during exertion (while running) plus an ejection systolic murmur is a red flag for left ventricular outflow obstruction, mainly hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or aortic stenosis. Echocardiography directly shows the structure (septal thickness, valve, outflow gradient), so it is the most appropriate test to establish the cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. ECG is a reasonable screening test and helps for arrhythmic causes (long QT, WPW), but it cannot define a structural lesion behind a murmur; it would be the key if the scenario pointed to an arrhythmia, for example palpitations with a normal exam.
C. Chest X-ray is nonspecific for heart size and lungs and cannot diagnose HCM or valve stenosis.
D. Reassurance fits a typical vasovagal faint at rest with an innocent murmur; exertional syncope with a murmur is never innocent.
key_concept:
Exertional syncope + systolic murmur = structural heart disease until proven otherwise; echo.
  • HCM: murmur louder with Valsalva or standing
  • Aortic stenosis: ejection murmur radiating to the carotids
  • Innocent murmur: asymptomatic, soft, systolic, changes with position
  • Arrhythmic causes (long QT, WPW): ECG
exam_pearl: Syncope at rest with prodrome is vasovagal; syncope DURING exercise is cardiac until proven otherwise.

stem: A child presented with low grade fever for 2 days then developed of acute onset of stridor What is the most common cause?
why_right: A low grade fever for 2 days (viral prodrome) followed by stridor is the typical course of croup (viral laryngotracheitis or laryngotracheobronchitis), most often due to parainfluenza virus. It is by far the most common cause of acute stridor in children.
why_wrong_block:
A. Epiglottitis is now rare and presents abruptly with high fever, a toxic look, drooling and tripod position, not a mild low grade prodrome.
B. Acute tonsillitis causes sore throat, fever and dysphagia but does not usually cause stridor unless complicated by a large abscess.
key_concept:
Viral prodrome + barking cough + inspiratory stridor in a well looking child = croup.
  • Cause: parainfluenza virus
  • Clinical diagnosis, no imaging needed
  • Treatment: steroids; nebulized epinephrine if distress
  • Toxic, drooling, tripod: epiglottitis, secure the airway
  • Toxic and not responding to croup treatment: bacterial tracheitis
  • Sudden choking, no prodrome: foreign body
exam_pearl: Low grade fever and a well child point to croup; high fever, drooling and a toxic look flip it to epiglottitis.

stem: A 3-year-old child with bronchial asthma on ventolin nebulizer at home as per needs. The mother expresses concern that the family cannot go out of the home most of the time because the nebulizer machine need electricity power source. Which of the following is the most appropriate counselling should be given?
OptA: Agree and support their decision as the priority is asthma control
OptB: Find someone to take care of asthmatic child if family goes out of the home
OptC: Educate with clear instructions inhaler usage and advice to stop nebulizer
OptD: Find out nebulizer machine with portability feature
highlight_terms_source: cannot go out of the home
why_right: Salbutamol given by metered dose inhaler with a spacer (plus face mask at age 3) is as effective as a nebulizer and is portable. Since the nebulizer needing electricity is restricting family life, the right counselling is to teach correct inhaler and spacer technique and stop the nebulizer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Accepting a confined lifestyle is unnecessary because equal asthma control is possible with a portable inhaler and spacer.
B. Arranging a caregiver does not fix the real problem (the device) and isolates the child from family life.
D. A portable nebulizer adds cost and still is not needed, since an inhaler with spacer is equally effective and already portable.
key_concept:
Children: MDI + spacer (with face mask if young) = nebulizer in effectiveness, and more practical.
  • Young child: MDI + spacer + face mask
  • Older child: MDI + spacer with mouthpiece
  • Poor control: check technique and adherence first
  • Frequent symptoms on SABA alone: add inhaled steroid
exam_pearl: Counselling questions reward the option that fixes the cause with equal efficacy, not the one that accommodates the problem.

stem: Picture of pediatric feet nails with koilonychia, the child presented with pallor, lethargy, and fatigue, CBC shows microcytic hypo-chromic RBC, What is the treatment ?
why_right: Koilonychia (spoon nails) with pallor, lethargy and fatigue and a microcytic hypochromic CBC is iron deficiency anemia. The lead in asks for treatment, and the first line treatment of IDA in a child who can take tablets or syrup is oral ferrous sulfate. Response is checked by a rise in reticulocytes and hemoglobin after starting oral iron.
why_wrong_block:
A. Parenteral iron is reserved for failure of oral iron: malabsorption (e.g. celiac or IBD), true intolerance or persistent nonadherence. Nothing here suggests oral therapy has failed.
C. Folic acid deficiency gives a megaloblastic macrocytic anemia; this smear is microcytic and hypochromic.
D. B12 deficiency is also macrocytic and may bring neurological signs; it does not cause spoon nails or a microcytic picture.
key_concept:
Microcytic hypochromic anemia plus koilonychia = iron deficiency; treat with oral ferrous sulfate first.
  • IDA signs: pallor, fatigue, pica, koilonychia, angular cheilitis, glossitis
  • IDA labs: low ferritin, MCV, MCH; high TIBC, RDW, platelets
  • High RDW favors IDA; normal RDW favors thalassemia trait
  • No response to adequate oral iron: think thalassemia, so do Hb electrophoresis
  • Parenteral iron only when oral fails or cannot be absorbed
exam_pearl: Microcytic anemia not improving on oral iron: check adherence and dosing first, then think thalassemia trait (normal RDW, do Hb electrophoresis); it is not an automatic switch to IV iron.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1443).
Compiler note: Bold option in screenshot (top of next page); photo of toenails with koilonychia.

stem: A 30 minute neonate at 27 weeks, delivered by emergency cesarean section for maternal reason have tachypnea, lobeared breathing and chest wall recession. Blood pressure 55/35 mmHg, Heart rate 135 /min, Respiratory rate 65/min, Temperature 36.2 C, Oxygen saturation 86 %. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 27 week preterm neonate at 30 minutes of life with tachypnea (RR 65), labored breathing, chest wall recession and SpO2 86% has respiratory distress syndrome. RDS is caused by surfactant deficiency in the immature lung and presents with severe distress from birth. The severity and the extreme prematurity outweigh the cesarean delivery clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pneumothorax is suggested by sudden deterioration, asymmetric breath sounds or ventilation; here distress is present from birth with no air leak clue.
B. Apnea of prematurity means pauses in breathing, usually starting after the first day or two, not continuous tachypnea with recession at 30 minutes.
D. TTN is a term cesarean baby with milder distress and fluid in the fissures on CXR that resolves on its own; severe hypoxia in a 27 week infant points to RDS.
key_concept:
Preterm + distress from birth + hypoxia = RDS; term C section + mild distress = TTN.
  • RDS: surfactant deficiency; CXR diffuse ground glass (reticulogranular)
  • TTN: retained fetal lung fluid; CXR perihilar streaks, fluid in fissure; self limiting
  • Antenatal corticosteroids are given to prevent RDS
  • Pneumothorax: sudden worsening, asymmetric chest
exam_pearl: C section is the TTN clue, but extreme prematurity with marked hypoxia overrides it in favor of RDS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Bold option in screenshot; neonatal CXR shown.

stem: 9 month boy on breast feeding , his mother recently started to introduce solid food , but he is mainly on breast feeding , what you recommend regarding his feeding:
OptD: speed up the rate of introduction of the solid food.
why_right: Iron stores from birth are largely used up by around 6 months, and breast milk contains little iron. A 9 month old who is still mainly breastfed with solids only just started is therefore at risk of iron deficiency, so iron supplementation is recommended until iron rich complementary foods are established. This is also why anemia screening is done at 9 to 12 months.
why_wrong_block:
B. Folate deficiency is uncommon in breastfed infants and routine folate supplementation is not recommended; folate is a pregnancy supplement for the mother.
C. Vitamin D is recommended for breastfed infants from birth as routine prophylaxis, but the specific risk this stem highlights (late, slow weaning at 9 months) is iron depletion.
D. Solids should be introduced gradually, one new food a few days apart to watch for reactions; rushing the pace does not reliably fix iron intake and is not the recommended advice.
key_concept:
Mainly breastfed infant beyond 6 months with limited solids = iron supplement.
  • Neonatal iron stores deplete by about 4 to 6 months
  • Breast milk is low in iron (and vitamin D)
  • Cow's milk before 12 months also causes IDA (occult GI loss, poor absorption)
  • CBC anemia screening at 9 to 12 months
  • Introduce each new food a few days apart
exam_pearl: If the stem stresses delayed or limited solids in a breastfed infant past 6 months, the answer is iron; vitamin D is the routine from birth answer.

stem: I had a question today about a 2-year-old kid who came with his mother. The chief complaint was that the kid's grandpa, who lives with them in the same house, was diagnosed with open tuberculosis. She's asking what we should do for the baby. The baby's medical history was almost positive for BCG vaccine.
OptA: Reassure because he already had the vaccine
OptB: Do chest X-ray and PPD and then wait for results.
OptC: Start them on isoniazid and ethambutol and typical TB treatment.
OptD: CXR + PPD + Start Latent TB Treatment NOW
why_right: A 2 year old living in the same house as a grandparent with open (infectious) TB is a high risk contact: young children progress quickly to severe disease such as TB meningitis or miliary TB. They are screened with CXR and tuberculin test to exclude active disease, and preventive (latent TB) therapy is started without waiting for the skin test result, because the test may be falsely negative early after exposure. BCG does not reliably prevent infection.
why_wrong_block:
A. BCG mainly reduces severe childhood forms of TB and does not prevent infection after close household exposure, so reassurance alone is unsafe.
B. Waiting for PPD results delays protection in a child under 5; the early test can be negative during the window period, so prophylaxis is started now and the test repeated later.
C. Multidrug therapy is for active TB, which has not been shown here (asymptomatic contact, CXR not yet done); this would be right if the CXR or symptoms showed active disease.
key_concept:
Child under 5 exposed to infectious TB: exclude active disease and start preventive therapy immediately.
  • Active TB on CXR or symptoms: full multidrug regimen
  • No active TB: latent TB regimen (e.g. isoniazid 6 months, rifampicin 4 months)
  • Recent contacts: TST ≥ 5 mm counts as positive
  • Initial negative TST in a young contact: continue prophylaxis and retest later
  • BCG history does not change contact management
exam_pearl: In young child contacts, do not wait for the PPD before starting prophylaxis; a prior BCG is never a reason to reassure.

stem: Child presented with fever, diarrhea, sunken eyes, poor feeding, hypotension, and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Which single finding most strongly indicates immediate admission?
why_right: Fever, diarrhea, sunken eyes and poor feeding describe dehydration, but hypotension with a capillary refill of 4 seconds shows impaired perfusion, i.e. shock. Prolonged capillary refill is the single listed finding that marks circulatory compromise, which needs admission and immediate IV fluid resuscitation rather than oral rehydration at home.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reduced appetite for solids is common in any sick child; only inability to take fluids or persistent vomiting would push toward admission.
B. Fever is a nonspecific feature of the infection and alone does not indicate severity or need for admission.
key_concept:
In pediatric dehydration, signs of poor perfusion (prolonged capillary refill over 2 s, weak pulse, hypotension, altered consciousness) mean severe dehydration or shock: admit and give IV boluses.
  • Mild: alert, normal eyes and pulse, skin pinch returns immediately
  • Moderate: irritable, sunken eyes, dry tongue, rapid pulse, slow skin pinch
  • Severe: drowsy, very sunken eyes, weak thready pulse, very slow skin pinch, scanty urine
  • Hypotension is a late sign in children
exam_pearl: In children, perfusion signs (capillary refill, pulse, mental state) outrank fever or appetite when deciding admission.

stem: Initial treatment for Hirschsprung disease?
why_right: The lead in is initial treatment. A child presenting with Hirschsprung obstruction is first stabilized: bowel decompression (rectal irrigations or washouts, nasogastric decompression), IV fluids and correction of electrolytes, with antibiotics if enterocolitis is present. Definitive surgery (resection of the aganglionic segment with a pull through) follows once the child is stable and the diagnosis is confirmed by rectal biopsy.
why_wrong_block: A. Surgical resection of the aganglionic segment is the definitive treatment, done electively after decompression and biopsy confirmation, not as an immediate first step; a total colectomy is not the standard operation.
key_concept:
Hirschsprung: decompress and stabilize first, then definitive pull through resection.
  • Clues: delayed meconium beyond 24 to 48 h, distension, bilious vomiting
  • DRE: tight sphincter, empty rectum, explosive gush of stool (squirt sign)
  • Initial imaging: AXR or contrast enema (transition zone)
  • Confirmatory test: rectal biopsy (absent ganglion cells)
  • Enterocolitis: fluids, decompression, antibiotics
exam_pearl: Read the verb: "initial" = decompression and support; "definitive" or "most appropriate management" = surgical resection.

stem: Child with enlarged tonsils and exudate. Brother also sick. Associated runny nose and conjunctivitis present. Most likely diagnosis?
key_concept:
Exudate alone does not separate viral from bacterial tonsillitis; the companions decide. The companion recall with this same scenario (AS-2068) is keyed to adenovirus pharyngitis.
  • Conjunctivitis + coryza + family cluster: adenovirus
  • Tender anterior nodes, no cough or coryza: group A strep
  • Generalized nodes, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes: EBV
  • Strep confirmed by rapid antigen test or throat culture
exam_pearl: Conjunctivitis plus runny nose pushes exudative tonsillitis toward a virus; their absence with tender anterior nodes favors strep.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No answer printed; see 2068 (same scenario, answer Adenovirus pharyngitis).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 5 year old child has red eye, headache, sore throat, and fever. On examination the patient has bilateral conjunctivitis and tonsillitis with exudates. His 2 year old brother had the same symptoms 2 days ago. What IS the likely cause? (No lymph node, no cough, no hepatosplenomegaly. no GI symptoms were mentioned)
highlight_terms_source: 2 year old brother had the same symptoms
why_right: Fever, sore throat and exudative tonsillitis together with bilateral conjunctivitis in a 5 year old, with a 2 year old brother who had the same illness 2 days earlier, is pharyngoconjunctival fever caused by adenovirus. Adenovirus spreads easily within households and causes conjunctivitis, pharyngitis and fever at any age. The absence of lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly argues against EBV.
why_wrong_block:
A. Kawasaki disease needs fever for 5 days or more with non exudative conjunctivitis, lip and tongue changes, extremity changes, rash or a cervical node; exudative tonsillitis and a sibling cluster point to infection instead.
B. Group A strep causes exudative tonsillitis with tender anterior nodes but not conjunctivitis; the conjunctivitis and rapid spread to a 2 year old favor a virus.
D. Infectious mononucleosis gives exudative tonsillitis with prominent lymphadenopathy, fatigue and often hepatosplenomegaly, mostly in adolescents; none of these are present and conjunctivitis is not typical.
key_concept:
Exudative tonsillitis + conjunctivitis + household spread = adenovirus (pharyngoconjunctival fever); management is supportive.
  • Adenovirus: conjunctivitis, pharyngitis, fever, gastroenteritis, croup, cystitis, pneumonia
  • Strep: tender anterior nodes, no cough or conjunctivitis
  • EBV: generalized nodes, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes
  • Kawasaki: fever ≥ 5 days, conjunctivitis without exudate, mucosal and extremity changes
exam_pearl: Conjunctivitis with exudative tonsillitis is adenovirus; conjunctivitis without exudate and prolonged fever is Kawasaki.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot (originally numbered 32) on next page; answer printed below options.

stem: Unvaccinated infant with meningitis. Gram-negative pleomorphic coccobacillus identified. Organism?
why_right: A gram negative pleomorphic coccobacillus in the CSF identifies Haemophilus influenzae. In an unvaccinated infant this is type b (Hib), which was a leading cause of infant meningitis before the Hib conjugate vaccine. The vaccination history is the second clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neisseria meningitidis is a gram negative diplococcus (kidney bean pairs), often with a petechial or purpuric rash; it is not a pleomorphic coccobacillus.
C. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram positive lancet shaped diplococcus; it is the commonest cause in vaccinated children and adults but does not match this Gram stain.
key_concept:
CSF Gram stain identifies the bacterium.
  • Gram negative coccobacilli: H. influenzae type b (unvaccinated)
  • Gram negative diplococci: N. meningitidis
  • Gram positive diplococci: S. pneumoniae
  • Gram positive rods: Listeria (neonates, elderly, immunocompromised)
  • Hib contacts: rifampicin prophylaxis
exam_pearl: Coccobacillus = Haemophilus; diplococcus = meningococcus (negative) or pneumococcus (positive).

stem: female 7y old with facial rash and multiple small joint tenderness suggestive of SLE. Marker of disease activity?
why_right: The question asks for a marker of disease activity, not a screening test. Anti dsDNA is specific for SLE and its titer rises with flares, particularly lupus nephritis, so it is used (with complement C3 and C4, which fall during activity) to monitor disease activity.
why_wrong_block:
A. ANA is the sensitive screening test for SLE; it stays positive regardless of activity and its titer does not track flares.
B. Rheumatoid factor is linked to rheumatoid arthritis and is nonspecific; it is neither diagnostic of nor a monitor for SLE.
key_concept:
SLE antibodies by role.
  • ANA: screening, most sensitive
  • Anti Smith: most specific
  • Anti dsDNA: specific and tracks disease activity (with low C3 and C4)
  • Anti histone: drug induced lupus
  • Antiphospholipid antibodies: thrombosis and pregnancy loss
exam_pearl: Screening = ANA, most specific = anti Smith, activity = anti dsDNA and complement.

stem: Child with severe epigastric pain, pancreatic edema on ultrasound, amylase 400 lipase 100 something, Best treatment?
why_right: Severe epigastric pain plus raised pancreatic enzymes plus pancreatic edema on ultrasound meets the 2 of 3 criteria for acute pancreatitis. Treatment is supportive: IV fluid resuscitation (Ringer lactate preferred) and adequate analgesia, with early feeding as tolerated. Nothing in the stem points to biliary obstruction or infection.
why_wrong_block: A. Antibiotics have no role in acute pancreatitis unless an infection is confirmed (e.g. infected necrosis), and ERCP is reserved for confirmed gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction; neither is described here.
key_concept:
Acute pancreatitis = 2 of 3: typical pain, amylase/lipase ≥3x normal, imaging findings.
  • Step 1: IV crystalloid (Ringer lactate), analgesia
  • Step 2: supportive care, early enteral feeding
  • Antibiotics: only for proven infection
  • ERCP: only biliary pancreatitis with cholangitis/obstruction
  • CT: if diagnosis unclear or to assess complications after 48 to 72 h
  • Children: trauma, drugs, viral, biliary and congenital anomalies are common causes
exam_pearl: Fluids and pain control first; ERCP and antibiotics are tempting distractors that need a specific indication.

stem: 4month old baby, presented with signs of UTI, stable not dehydrated. Alert and feeding we Urinalysis: Positive nitrite., Positive leukocytes., Fever: 39.1 What's the appropriate empirical antibiotic to be started?
why_right: Febrile UTI (fever 39.1, nitrite and leukocyte esterase positive) in a 4 month old who is stable, alert, feeding well and not dehydrated. Infants older than about 2 months who are not toxic and tolerate oral intake can be treated orally, with outcomes equal to IV therapy. Of the options, oral amoxicillin is the only oral agent aimed at uropathogens, so it is the keyed choice.
why_wrong_block:
A. Azithromycin (a macrolide) does not reliably cover Gram negative uropathogens such as E. coli and is not used for UTI.
C. IV ceftriaxone is for infants younger than about 2 months, toxic appearance, vomiting or inability to tolerate oral intake; this infant is alert and feeding well.
D. IV cefepime is a broad spectrum antipseudomonal agent reserved for severe or resistant infection; a mild febrile UTI does not need it.
key_concept:
Pediatric febrile UTI: route depends on age and how sick the child looks.
  • Older than 2 to 3 months, well, tolerating orals: oral (cephalexin, cefixime, amoxicillin per local resistance)
  • Young infant, toxic, vomiting, dehydrated: IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime
  • Urinalysis clues: nitrite, leukocyte esterase, pyuria
  • Gold standard: urine culture (catheter or suprapubic sample)
exam_pearl: Same infant but vomiting, lethargic or under 2 months flips the answer to IV ceftriaxone.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' screenshot under 2080 (starts on next page). Oral amoxicillin circled in red pen and highlighted; IV Ceftriaxone struck through. Answer: B. Attached reference: Management of acute infection: most children can be treated with oral antibiotics, but infants...

stem: 4-year-old comes with 1 month history of non-bloody diarrhea, it only occurs in daytime and not at night, the patient appears well and no failure to thrive.
highlight_terms_source: only occurs in daytime and not at night
why_right: Chronic (1 month) non-bloody loose stools in a 4-year-old who looks well with no failure to thrive, occurring in the daytime and not at night, is the classic picture of toddler's diarrhea (functional diarrhea). It is linked to high fruit juice and low fat intake and settles with dietary advice; growth stays normal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Rotavirus causes acute watery diarrhea with vomiting and fever, mainly under 2 years, lasting days rather than a month.
C. Salmonella causes acute febrile diarrhea, often with blood or mucus and systemic upset, not a month of daytime-only stools in a well child.
key_concept:
Chronic diarrhea in a thriving child = functional until proven otherwise.
  • Toddler's diarrhea: 1 to 5 years, daytime only, undigested food in stool, normal growth
  • Celiac: failure to thrive, distension, buttock wasting after gluten
  • IBD: weight loss, blood, nocturnal symptoms
  • Infective (rota, salmonella): acute, febrile
exam_pearl: Nocturnal diarrhea or poor growth points away from toddler's diarrhea toward organic disease.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed version lists only A. Toddler's diarrhea B. Rotavirus with no answer; embedded screenshot gives Answer: A.

stem: A 2-year-old child initially had upper respiratory tract infection / viral symptoms. After around 12 hours, the child presented to the ER with cyanosis, drooling, tripod position, and oxygen saturation of 88%. What is the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: upper respiratory tract infection / viral symptoms
why_right: This recall's key is bacterial tracheitis because the child first had viral URTI symptoms and then deteriorated over hours to severe obstruction (cyanosis, SpO2 88%, tripod posture). Bacterial tracheitis is a secondary bacterial infection (often S. aureus) of the trachea following a viral illness or croup, producing thick purulent membranes and a toxic child who does not respond to croup treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Croup gives barking cough and stridor in a usually well looking child after a URTI; cyanosis, drooling and tripod position are not expected and would signal failure.
B. Epiglottitis classically gives drooling, tripod position and toxicity, but it starts abruptly in a previously well child without a viral prodrome and is now rare after Hib vaccination.
key_concept:
Upper airway emergencies in children:
  • Croup: viral prodrome, barking cough, stridor, well looking
  • Bacterial tracheitis: viral prodrome then sudden toxic deterioration, poor response to epinephrine
  • Epiglottitis: abrupt high fever, drooling, tripod, muffled voice, no cough
  • All severe cases: secure airway first
exam_pearl: Viral prodrome then sudden toxic decline = tracheitis; abrupt onset with drooling in a previously well child = epiglottitis.

stem: A pediatric patient came to the well clinic with only runny nose and cough. Temperature was 36.5°C. What should be done regarding vaccination?
why_right: The child has only a runny nose and cough with a normal temperature (36.5°C). A mild illness with or without low grade fever is not a contraindication to any vaccine, including live vaccines, so the scheduled vaccines should be given today. Postponing only creates missed opportunities.
why_wrong_block:
B. Postponing is for a moderate or severe acute illness (e.g. high fever, ill child); a simple cold does not justify delay.
C. Withholding live vaccines is for immunosuppression or pregnancy (and timing after blood products), not for a minor URTI.
key_concept:
Vaccinate unless there is a true contraindication or precaution.
  • Give: mild URTI, low grade fever, antibiotics, recent exposure, prematurity
  • Postpone: moderate to severe acute illness
  • Contraindicated: anaphylaxis to prior dose or component
  • Avoid live vaccines: immunocompromise, pregnancy
exam_pearl: A cold is not a reason to delay vaccination; only moderate to severe illness is.

stem: 7 year-old child unvaccinated presents with mild fever and cropped vesicles on the trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis? Vitals weren't given
why_right: An unvaccinated child with mild fever and vesicles appearing in crops on the trunk (central distribution, lesions at different stages) is chickenpox caused by varicella zoster virus. It is a clinical diagnosis, confirmable by PCR if needed.
why_wrong_block:
B. HSV-1 in children causes gingivostomatitis: painful vesicles and ulcers on the lips, gums and mouth with cervical nodes, not crops of truncal vesicles.
C. Smallpox is eradicated; its lesions were all at the same stage and concentrated on the face and limbs (centrifugal).
D. Measles gives a maculopapular (not vesicular) rash starting on the face with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots.
key_concept:
Vesicular rash in a child:
  • Varicella: crops, different stages, starts on trunk/face then spreads, itchy
  • Smallpox: same stage, centrifugal, deep lesions
  • HSV-1: perioral and gingival vesicles
  • Hand foot mouth: oral ulcers plus hands and feet
  • Measles: maculopapular, Koplik spots
exam_pearl: Lesions at different stages = varicella; all at the same stage = smallpox.

stem: Child present with meconium aspiration and shortness of breath, was managed by mechanical intubation. how to diagnose complications?
why_right: Meconium aspiration requiring mechanical ventilation is a classic setting for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), with right-to-left shunting through the ductus and foramen ovale. The diagnostic test for this complication is echocardiography, which shows raised pulmonary pressures and the shunt and excludes structural heart disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bronchoscopy is not used to diagnose complications of meconium aspiration; it has a role mainly for suspected airway foreign body or structural airway lesions.
C. Lung ultrasound can show parenchymal changes or pneumothorax but cannot assess pulmonary artery pressure or ductal shunting.
D. ECG may show right ventricular strain but is neither sensitive nor specific for PPHN.
key_concept:
Complications of meconium aspiration and how to find them:
  • PPHN: pre-ductal SpO2 higher than post-ductal, confirm by echo, treat with inhaled nitric oxide
  • Pneumothorax (air leak on ventilation): chest X-ray
  • Chemical pneumonitis, surfactant inactivation
exam_pearl: Pre/post-ductal saturation gap in a ventilated meconium baby = PPHN; confirm with echo.

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents to the ER with abnormal movements during sleep involving his face and limbs. He has a history of seizures but is otherwise neurologically normal. EEG shows frontotemporal spikes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 7-year-old, neurologically normal, with seizures during sleep involving the face (and limbs) and temporal region spikes on EEG is benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (rolandic epilepsy). It peaks in school age, usually starts focal in the face and mouth with drooling or speech arrest, may generalize at night, and remits by adolescence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Infantile spasms (West syndrome) occur in infants with clusters of flexor or extensor spasms, developmental regression and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
B. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy starts in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks after waking, and generalized polyspike and wave on EEG.
key_concept:
Childhood epilepsy syndromes by age and EEG:
  • Infantile spasms: infancy, hypsarrhythmia
  • Absence: 5 to 8 years, staring, 3 Hz spike and wave
  • Rolandic: school age, nocturnal facial seizures, centrotemporal spikes, normal child
  • JME: adolescence, morning myoclonus, polyspike and wave
exam_pearl: Nocturnal facial twitching in a normal school-age child = rolandic; morning jerks in a teenager = JME.

stem: A 5-day-old girl brought to Emergency Room with lethargy and poor feeding. On examination, she was irritable, deeply jaundiced and dehydrated. The mother gave history of previous babies' required admission and exchange transfusion (see lab results). Which of the following is important to be obtained in the history? Blood pressure 90/55 mmHg, Heart rate 95 /min, Respiratory rate 18 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 94 %, Weight 3 kg. Hb 95 (165-195 g/L newborn); Reticulocyte 3 (0.2-1.2 %); Total bilirubin 360 (<205 mol/L term 3-5 days).
highlight_terms_source: previous babies' required admission and exchange transfusion
why_right: Day 5 neonate with deep jaundice (bilirubin 360), anemia (Hb 95) and raised reticulocytes (3%) has a hemolytic picture. Previous babies needing exchange transfusion points to recurrent isoimmune hemolytic disease, typically Rh alloimmunization worsening with each pregnancy. Maternal blood group (with the baby's group and a direct Coombs test) is the key history item.
why_wrong_block:
A. Apgar score reflects transition and asphyxia at birth; it does not explain hemolysis recurring across siblings.
B. Birth weight does not explain a familial hemolytic anemia with jaundice.
C. Type of delivery may relate to bruising or cephalohematoma, but not to recurrent hemolysis requiring exchange transfusion in siblings.
key_concept:
Neonatal jaundice plus anemia plus reticulocytosis = hemolysis.
  • Ask: maternal and baby blood groups (Rh, ABO), anti-D history
  • Test: direct Coombs
  • Rh disease: worsens in successive pregnancies
  • ABO: can affect the first baby, usually milder
  • Others: G6PD deficiency, spherocytosis
exam_pearl: Siblings who needed exchange transfusion is the classic Rh isoimmunization clue.

stem: An 18-month-old child with normal growth and weight 50th percentile is brought by his parents. They are concerned because his older sibling was recently diagnosed with celiac disease. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: This recall's key is reassurance because the 18-month-old is asymptomatic with normal growth (50th percentile); a sibling's diagnosis raises risk but does not make this child ill. Screening of well first-degree relatives is usually deferred until about 2 to 3 years of age, after adequate gluten exposure, so nothing is needed today beyond reassurance and a plan to test later or sooner if symptoms appear. A gluten free diet must never be started without a confirmed diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. tTG-IgA (with total IgA) is the right first test when there are celiac symptoms (diarrhea, distension, failure to thrive), or as screening of an at-risk relative once older (about 2 to 3 years); this toddler is well and young, so testing can wait.
C. Starting a gluten free diet without serology and biopsy is wrong: it is unnecessary in a healthy child and causes false negative results if testing is later needed.
key_concept:
Celiac disease workup:
  • Symptoms or failure to thrive: tTG-IgA (with total IgA) while on gluten
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (do not stop gluten before)
  • Treatment: gluten free diet only after diagnosis
  • At-risk groups: first-degree relatives, type 1 diabetes, Down, Turner syndromes
exam_pearl: Never start a gluten free diet before testing; it masks the diagnosis.

stem: An 4-Year-Old child with normal growth and weight is brought by his parents. They are concerned because his older sibling has celiac disease. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: First-degree relatives of a patient with celiac disease are at high risk and should be screened even when asymptomatic. This child with "normal growth and weight" whose "older sibling has celiac disease" should have tTG IgA, the initial screening serology, while still eating gluten.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance misses a high-risk child; normal growth does not exclude celiac disease, which can be silent in relatives.
C. Starting a gluten-free diet before testing is wrong: gluten withdrawal makes serology and biopsy falsely negative, and diet is only started after the diagnosis is confirmed.
key_concept:
Celiac disease: serology, then biopsy, then diet.
  • Screen first-degree relatives and type 1 diabetes even without symptoms
  • Initial test: tTG IgA (with total IgA)
  • Confirm: endoscopy with duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia)
  • Test while on gluten
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten-free diet; tTG also monitors compliance
exam_pearl: Never start a gluten-free diet before serology and biopsy; it produces false-negative results.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0584).

stem: A 53-day-old boy is referred to the Paediatric Clinic for investigation of anaemia. He was born full term and he is a known case of G6PD deficiency. On examination, both height and weight are in the 10th percentile, the rest of the examination is normal (see lab results). Hb 70 (112-165 g/L); Platelet count 350 (150-400 x 109/L); Total bilirubin 25.1 (<20.5 mol/L). Urinalysis: Color clear; Leukocytes 0 (0-3/hpf); Erythrocytes 0 (0-2/hpf). Which of the following is the best management?
why_right: A term infant at 53 days (about 8 weeks) is at the age of the physiological Hb nadir, which falls at 8 to 12 weeks. The rest of the exam is normal and the urinalysis is clear with no blood, so there is no sign of an active hemolytic episode despite the known G6PD deficiency. The recall therefore treats this as physiological anemia of infancy, which recovers on its own as erythropoietin rises, so the keyed management is reassurance with follow up.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood transfusion: kept for a symptomatic infant (poor feeding, tachycardia, heart failure) or a severe acute hemolytic crisis; this baby is well with a normal exam. It is the main competing option because Hb 70 is lower than the usual nadir.
B. Iron supplement: a term baby has enough iron stores for the first 4 to 6 months, so iron deficiency is not the cause at 53 days; iron is right for an older infant on cow's milk with microcytosis.
D. Folic acid: there is no clue to megaloblastic anemia or folate deficiency; folate is given in chronic hemolytic states with high red cell turnover, not physiological anemia.
key_concept:
Well term infant at 8 to 12 weeks with isolated anemia and normal exam = physiological anemia of infancy: reassure and follow.
  • Term nadir: about 9 to 11 g/dL at 8 to 12 weeks
  • Preterm nadir: deeper and earlier, 3 to 6 weeks
  • Mechanism: high Hb at birth suppresses erythropoietin, then hypoxia switches it back on
  • G6PD hemolysis needs a trigger plus jaundice and dark urine
  • Term iron stores last 4 to 6 months
exam_pearl: Known G6PD deficiency is a distractor here: clear urine, no trigger and a normal exam point away from hemolysis.

stem: 6days new born with g6pd def. Type of anemia?
why_right: This recall is keyed to physiological anemia, the same teaching point as the related 53-day G6PD infant case: in a well term baby with known G6PD deficiency and no trigger, the drop in Hb is the normal postnatal fall, not disease. After birth the high fetal Hb declines because erythropoietin is suppressed by better oxygenation, and it recovers without treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hemolytic: right if there is a trigger (fava beans, infection, oxidant drugs) with jaundice, pallor and dark urine or hemoglobinuria; the known G6PD deficiency alone is the trap.
B. Inflammatory: needs an active infection or inflammatory illness, which is not described in this newborn.
C. Of chronic disease: needs a long-standing chronic illness (renal, inflammatory, malignancy); it does not fit a newborn.
key_concept:
G6PD infant with anemia but no trigger, no hemoglobinuria and a normal exam = physiological anemia, not hemolysis.
  • Term nadir at 8 to 12 weeks, Hb about 9 to 11 g/dL
  • Preterm nadir earlier (3 to 6 weeks) and deeper
  • G6PD hemolysis: trigger, jaundice, dark urine, bite or Heinz bodies
  • Neonatal G6PD often presents as early jaundice
exam_pearl: Physiological anemia is timed by age: the classic nadir is weeks 8 to 12, so check the age in the stem before choosing it.

stem: A 53-day-old boy is referred to the Paediatric Clinic for investigation of anemia. He was born at full term and he is a known case of G6PD deficiency. On examination, both height and weight are in the 10th percentile, the rest of the examination is normal (see lab results). Hb 70 (112-165 g/L); Platelet count 350 (150-400 x 109/L); Total bilirubin 25.1 (<20.5 mol/L). Urinalysis: Color clear; Leukocytes 0; Erythrocytes 0. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: This recall's key is the physiological option: a term boy at 53 days is at the physiological Hb nadir (8 to 12 weeks), the exam is otherwise normal and the urinalysis is clear with no blood, so the picture is a normal postnatal process rather than disease. The same case in the source is keyed to physiological anemia of infancy; read option C as that concept.
why_wrong_block:
A. Haemolysis: right with a trigger plus jaundice, pallor and dark urine or hemoglobinuria; here the urine is clear and the exam normal, so the known G6PD deficiency is a distractor.
B. Iron deficiency: term infants have adequate iron stores until about 4 to 6 months; it fits an older infant on cow's milk with low MCV.
D. Anaemia of chronic disease: needs a chronic inflammatory, renal or malignant illness, which this well infant does not have.
key_concept:
Well term infant at 8 to 12 weeks with isolated anemia = physiological anemia of infancy.
  • Term nadir: about 9 to 11 g/dL at 8 to 12 weeks
  • Physiological jaundice: starts after 24 h, resolves by about 2 weeks in term babies
  • Jaundice beyond 2 weeks (term) = prolonged, needs conjugated bilirubin
  • G6PD hemolysis: trigger, jaundice, dark urine
exam_pearl: The diagnosis being tested is physiological ANEMIA; physiological jaundice is over by 2 weeks in a term baby.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot under 2118 at top of next page (same case as 2117 but asking diagnosis); Answer: C.

stem: A 14-year-old female presents for evaluation of delayed puberty. Physical examination reveals Tanner Stage 1 for both breast development and pubic hair. Laboratory investigations show normal levels of FSH and LH, but a mildly elevated serum estradiol level. Given this clinical picture, which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
highlight_terms_source: normal levels of FSH and LH
key_concept:
Delayed puberty in a girl: first check FSH and LH.
  • High FSH/LH, low estradiol: primary ovarian failure (Turner most common)
  • Low or normal FSH/LH: constitutional delay, chronic illness, low weight, hypothalamic or pituitary causes
  • Precocious puberty: signs before age 8 in girls
  • Central = pubertal LH/FSH; peripheral = suppressed LH/FSH with high sex steroids
  • Tanner 1 breast = prepubertal
exam_pearl: Delayed (not precocious) puberty with short stature in a girl makes Turner the exam favourite, but it needs HIGH gonadotropins.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 8 years old, boy bed witting No hx of UTI. What's the best next step ?
OptC: Train with a bedtime alarm or something like that. ( NO REASSURANCE )
why_right: An 8-year-old with bedwetting and no history of UTI is primary nocturnal enuresis with no red flags. Once simple behavioural measures (fluid timing, voiding before bed, rewards, no punishment) are in place, the enuresis alarm is the first-line active treatment, with the best long-term cure and lowest relapse rate. The recall also stresses that plain reassurance alone is not the answer at this age.
why_wrong_block:
A. Refer to psychiatry: enuresis is a developmental delay in bladder control, not a psychiatric illness; referral fits only when there are clear emotional or behavioural problems or abuse concerns.
B. Give Desmopressin: oral desmopressin is used when the alarm fails or is unsuitable, or for quick short-term dryness (sleepovers, camps); relapse after stopping is common, and the intranasal form is avoided because of hyponatremia.
key_concept:
Primary nocturnal enuresis, no red flags: behavioural advice, then alarm, then desmopressin.
  • Under about 5 to 6 years: reassurance
  • Behavioural: fluid timing, void before bed, star chart, no punishment
  • Alarm: best long-term cure, needs a motivated family
  • Desmopressin: oral only, short-term or alarm failure
  • Red flags (daytime symptoms, UTI, polyuria, weight loss): urinalysis and workup first
exam_pearl: Reassurance alone fits a child under about 6; an 8-year-old needs active treatment, and the alarm comes before desmopressin.

stem: 3 years old, looks acutely ill, sit on his mother's lap with his neck extended. What is the management?
why_right: A 3-year-old who looks acutely ill and sits on the mother's lap with the neck extended (sniffing or tripod posture) is acute epiglottitis until proven otherwise. The airway can obstruct completely at any moment, so the priority is to keep the child calm and secure the airway by intubation in the operating room by the most experienced anaesthetist, with ENT ready for a surgical airway. Antibiotics are given once the airway is safe.
why_wrong_block:
A. Give him racemic epinephrine: nebulized epinephrine treats moderate to severe croup (barking cough, stridor in a child who looks well); in epiglottitis it does not fix the obstruction and the procedure can upset the child and precipitate complete obstruction.
B. dexamethasone: the mainstay of croup, which presents with a barking cough after URTI symptoms in a non-toxic child; it does not secure the airway in a toxic child with epiglottitis.
key_concept:
Toxic child + drooling + sniffing/tripod posture = epiglottitis: secure the airway in the OR first.
  • Do not lie the child down, examine the throat or take blood first
  • Keep with parent, calm, give oxygen as tolerated
  • Airway by senior anaesthetist in OR, ENT on standby
  • Then IV third-generation cephalosporin
  • Croup: barking cough, looks well, dexamethasone ± nebulized epinephrine
exam_pearl: Barking cough in a well child = croup (steroids); toxic, drooling, neck extended and silent = epiglottitis (airway in the OR).

stem: 5 yrs old boy with SVT, what is the initial investigation?
why_right: The lead-in asks for the initial investigation in a child with SVT. A 12-lead ECG is first: it confirms the narrow complex regular tachycardia, guides acute treatment (vagal manoeuvres, adenosine, cardioversion if unstable), and after conversion can show a delta wave of pre-excitation (WPW); an accessory pathway (AVRT) is the commonest SVT mechanism in children.
why_wrong_block: A. Echo: done later to look for structural heart disease or tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (for example in recurrent or prolonged SVT); it does not diagnose the rhythm and is not the first test.
key_concept:
Any suspected tachyarrhythmia: 12-lead ECG first, then targeted tests.
  • ECG during SVT: narrow complex, regular, P waves hidden or retrograde
  • ECG in sinus rhythm: look for delta wave (WPW)
  • Unstable: synchronized cardioversion
  • Stable: vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine
  • Echo: structural disease, ventricular function
  • Holter: intermittent palpitations with a normal resting ECG
exam_pearl: Echo answers 'is the heart structurally normal'; only the ECG answers 'what is the rhythm', so it always comes first.

stem: A 9-year-old child with gastroenteritis caused by Shigella species. Which of the following antibiotics should be prescribed?
why_right: This recall's key is ceftriaxone: in a child with Shigella gastroenteritis, fluoroquinolones were traditionally avoided and widespread ampicillin and co-trimoxazole resistance makes older drugs unreliable, so a third-generation cephalosporin is a standard choice, particularly for severe or invasive disease or a child who cannot take oral treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amoxicillin: Shigella resistance to ampicillin and amoxicillin is widespread and amoxicillin is poorly effective even for sensitive strains; not recommended.
C. Azithromycin: a recognised oral option for Shigella in children and the drug of choice for Campylobacter dysentery; it is the strongest competitor here (see note).
D. Metronidazole: covers anaerobes and protozoa (Giardia, Entamoeba, C. difficile), not Shigella.
key_concept:
Bacterial dysentery: match the organism to the antibiotic.
  • Shigella, child: azithromycin (oral) or ceftriaxone (parenteral, severe)
  • Shigella, adult: ciprofloxacin
  • Campylobacter: azithromycin
  • Giardia, amoebiasis, C. difficile: metronidazole
  • Shigella clue: bloody diarrhea with fever, febrile seizures in children
exam_pearl: Bloody diarrhea plus a seizure in a child points to Shigella; metronidazole is the trap answer for Giardia.

stem: Case of enlarged parotid gland bilaterally (it was long) what's the causative organism?
why_right: Bilateral parotid enlargement lasting for days is classic for mumps, a paramyxovirus whose most common manifestation is parotitis, often painful and starting on one side before becoming bilateral, after a short prodrome of fever and malaise. It is the commonest infectious cause of bilateral parotid swelling, especially in an unvaccinated child.
why_wrong_block:
B. EBV: causes infectious mononucleosis with exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes; parotid swelling is uncommon.
C. CMV: usually a mild mononucleosis-like illness or congenital infection (deafness, periventricular calcifications); parotitis is rare, mainly in immunocompromised patients.
key_concept:
Bilateral painful parotid swelling with fever = mumps.
  • Mumps virus: paramyxovirus, prevented by MMR
  • Complications: orchitis (post-pubertal), aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, deafness
  • Unilateral, red, pus from Stensen duct = bacterial (S. aureus) parotitis
  • Other viral causes: parainfluenza, influenza, EBV, HIV
exam_pearl: Unilateral parotid swelling with pus from the duct in a dehydrated or postoperative patient is bacterial (S. aureus), not mumps.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A related screenshot follows on the next page (organ most commonly affected by mumps; see 2140b).

stem: Which of the following organs is most commonly affected by mumps in a 4-year-old boy?
why_right: The parotid gland is the organ most commonly affected by mumps: parotitis is its hallmark and is often bilateral and painful. In a 4-year-old (prepubertal) boy, the testes are rarely involved, so parotid clearly wins.
why_wrong_block:
A. Skin: mumps does not typically cause a rash; think measles, rubella or varicella for viral rashes.
B. Lungs: pneumonia is not a feature of mumps; measles is the viral exanthem with pneumonia as a leading complication.
C. Testes: orchitis is the commonest complication in post-pubertal males (it can affect fertility), but it is rare before puberty, so it is the answer only if the stem asks about an adolescent or adult male's complication.
key_concept:
Mumps: parotitis is the most common manifestation; complications depend on age.
  • Parotitis: most common, often bilateral
  • Orchitis: mainly post-pubertal males
  • Aseptic meningitis: most common CNS involvement
  • Also pancreatitis, sensorineural deafness
  • Prevented by MMR
exam_pearl: Organ most affected = parotid; most common complication in an adult male = orchitis; read whether the stem asks for the organ or the complication.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot shown under 2140; D highlighted and 'Answer: D'.

stem: A 6-month-old infant presents to the Emergency Room with sudden apnea and color change. The mother gave history of recurrent vomiting, and muitiple chest infection. On examination, he looks failing to thrive with dystonic neck posturing while crying. Which of the following considers as high-risk case for the above disease?
why_right: The picture is infant GERD: "recurrent vomiting" plus "multiple chest infection" (aspiration), "failing to thrive", apnea/color change (ALTE/BRUE from reflux) and "dystonic neck posturing" (Sandifer syndrome). Preterm infants are the classic high-risk group because their lower esophageal sphincter is immature, with more transient inappropriate relaxations.
why_wrong_block:
A. Obesity is a GERD risk factor in older children and adults, not the recognized high-risk group in infancy.
C. Pertussis causes paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting and apnea, but a past pertussis infection is not a recognized risk factor for infant reflux or Sandifer syndrome.
D. Hernia repair is not linked to GERD; post-anesthesia apnea risk after hernia repair relates to prematurity itself, not reflux.
key_concept:
Infant GERD with complications: vomiting + aspiration + FTT + Sandifer posturing.
  • Sandifer syndrome = dystonic neck/back arching from reflux, mimics seizures
  • Mechanism: transient inappropriate LES relaxation
  • High-risk groups: preterm, neurologic impairment (e.g. cerebral palsy), repaired esophageal atresia/TEF, chronic lung disease
  • Red flags: apnea, aspiration pneumonia, failure to thrive
exam_pearl: Dystonic neck posturing in a vomiting infant is reflux (Sandifer), not a seizure or torticollis; prematurity is the risk factor.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot marks **B; compiler's line: 'Answer: Preterm infant'.

stem: A child enters the clinic and says "hi" to the doctor then turns to the mother and says "milk". The mother gives her a bottle of milk, and the child tries to give her doll a drink. The mother shakes her head, and the child says "no". After which the child smiles and points to her own mouth and says "mouth". When her mother wipes the doll's face, the child says "me" and begins to imitate the mother's action and gives the doll a hug. What developmental age in months is this most consistent with?
why_right: The child uses several meaningful single words ("hi", "milk", "no", "mouth", "me"), points to and names a body part, and shows pretend play (feeding and hugging the doll). A vocabulary of about 6 to 10 single words with no 2-word phrases places her at 18 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 12 months imitation and 1 to 3 words fit, but naming a body part and a 6 to 10 word vocabulary come later.
B. At 15 months a child points to body parts and has a few words, but this many single words with pretend play fits 18 months.
D. At 24 months expect 2-word phrases ("me milk") and about 50 words; this child uses single words only.
key_concept:
Language milestones set the age when words are counted.
  • 12 mo: 1 to 3 words (mama/dada specific), imitation
  • 15 mo: few words, points to a body part
  • 18 mo: 6 to 10 single words, names a body part, pretend play
  • 24 mo: 2-word phrases, ~50 words
  • 36 mo: 3-word sentences
exam_pearl: Many single words but no 2-word phrase = 18 months; the first 2-word phrase moves it to 24 months.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot marks *C; compiler's line: 'Answer: 18'.

stem: Child 9 yrs has bed wetting and mother mentioned that he was dry since the age of six years. His mother noticed foul smelling urine and change in urine color. There is positive nitrite and leukocytes. Culture: gram negative bacilli bacteria. WBCs > 100,000. What is the most common organism causing this condition?
highlight_terms_source: dry since the age of six years
why_right: Secondary enuresis ("dry since the age of six"), foul smelling discolored urine, positive nitrite and leukocytes and a Gram negative bacillus at >100,000 CFU/ml confirm a UTI. E. coli is by far the most common cause of pediatric UTI (roughly 80 to 90 percent).
why_wrong_block:
B. Proteus is a urease producer (alkaline urine, struvite stones), more typical in uncircumcised boys or stone disease; it is a less common cause than E. coli.
C. Klebsiella is a Gram negative cause of UTI but much less common, seen more in hospital acquired or complicated infections.
D. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram positive coccus causing pneumonia, otitis and meningitis, not a urinary pathogen with Gram negative bacilli.
key_concept:
New bedwetting after being dry = secondary enuresis; rule out UTI, diabetes, stress.
  • Most common UTI organism: E. coli
  • Nitrite positive = Gram negative (nitrate reducing) bacteria
  • Significant bacteriuria on clean catch: >100,000 CFU/ml of one organism
  • Proteus: alkaline urine, struvite stones
exam_pearl: Secondary enuresis is a symptom, not a diagnosis; dipstick nitrite + leukocytes points to UTI, and the bug is E. coli.

stem: 6 months boy delivered full term vaginally without complications. Come to assess by doctor and he found him has normal development. Which of the following of gross motor development present in the infant at this age
why_right: This recall's key is sit without support because many milestone tables list sitting (initially tripod, with hand support) as the 6-month gross motor skill of a normal term infant. It is the option that defines the age, as opposed to an earlier skill already achieved.
why_wrong_block:
B. Rolling prone to supine appears around 4 months, so it is present at 6 months but is an earlier milestone, not the one that characterizes this age.
C. Mature (pincer) grasp is a fine motor skill appearing around 9 to 12 months; at 6 months the grasp is a palmar (raking) grasp.
key_concept:
Gross motor ladder in infancy.
  • 4 mo: rolls prone to supine, head steady
  • 5 to 6 mo: rolls supine to prone (both ways)
  • 6 mo: sits with tripod support; fully independent sitting about 7 to 9 mo
  • 9 mo: pulls to stand, stands holding support, pincer grasp starts
  • 12 mo: walks
exam_pearl: "Rolls supine to prone" and "tripod sitting" are both 6-month answers; prone to supine is 4 months, pincer grasp is 9 months and fine motor.

stem: Child came complaining of generalised edema and fatigue, he had history of bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain 2 weeks ago. Lab: Retics 3, Hb 9 or 8, Plt 55, Wbc 8, Cr high. What test would lead to diagnosis?
why_right: "Bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain 2 weeks ago" followed by edema, anemia (Hb 8 to 9 with reticulocytosis), thrombocytopenia (Plt 55) and high creatinine is post-diarrheal (typical) HUS. The test that establishes the cause is a stool study: culture for Shiga toxin producing E. coli (O157:H7) and Shiga toxin detection.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood tests (smear for schistocytes, LDH, haptoglobin, Coombs) confirm microangiopathic hemolysis and are part of the workup, but they do not identify the triggering infection.
B. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria reflecting the renal injury, but it is nonspecific and does not establish the etiology.
key_concept:
HUS triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury.
  • Typical: about 1 to 2 weeks after bloody diarrhea, STEC O157:H7 (also Shigella)
  • Etiology: stool culture / Shiga toxin
  • Smear: schistocytes; Coombs negative; normal PT/APTT (vs DIC)
  • Management: supportive (fluids, dialysis if needed); avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs
exam_pearl: Normal coagulation separates HUS from DIC; the history of bloody diarrhea sends you to the stool.

stem: Child came complaining reduced oral intake, expiratory wheeze, nasal discharge, and mild distress, no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A child with "nasal discharge" (URTI prodrome), "expiratory wheeze", "reduced oral intake" and "mild distress" with "no fever" fits viral bronchiolitis (most often RSV) in an infant. Diffuse expiratory wheeze reflects small airway obstruction and air trapping.
why_wrong_block: A. Pneumonia usually presents with fever, tachypnea and focal crackles or bronchial breathing; diffuse wheeze without fever points away from it.
key_concept:
Bronchiolitis: first wheezing episode with coryza in a child under 2 (peak under 1 year).
  • Cause: RSV most common
  • Signs: coryza, cough, wheeze and/or fine crackles, poor feeding, retractions
  • Fever often low grade or absent
  • Diagnosis is clinical; management supportive (O2 if low SpO2, hydration, suction)
  • Recurrent wheeze in an older child: think asthma
exam_pearl: Wheeze plus coryza in an infant without high fever is bronchiolitis; focal signs with high fever is pneumonia.

stem: Pediatric with seizure and Fatigue other signs, Hepatomegaly and Cataract Blood Culture: E.coli labs showed metabolic acidosis urine analysis: aminoaciduria and glycosuria What's the diagnosis?
why_right: "Hepatomegaly", "cataract" and E. coli sepsis are the classic triad clue for galactosemia (GALT deficiency). Accumulated galactose-1-phosphate damages the liver and renal tubules (Fanconi picture: "aminoaciduria and glycosuria" with metabolic acidosis), galactitol causes cataract, and hypoglycemia can cause seizures.
why_wrong_block:
B. Homocystinuria causes lens dislocation (downward), marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability and thrombosis, not cataract with liver failure and E. coli sepsis.
C. Methylmalonic acidemia causes severe anion gap metabolic acidosis with ketosis and hyperammonemia, but not cataract, Fanconi syndrome or E. coli sepsis.
D. Maple syrup urine disease presents with poor feeding, encephalopathy and burnt sugar smelling urine; it lacks cataract and hepatomegaly.
key_concept:
Galactosemia (classic, GALT deficiency, autosomal recessive).
  • Onset after milk feeding: vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive
  • Cataract (galactitol), renal Fanconi (aminoaciduria, glycosuria, acidosis)
  • E. coli neonatal sepsis is a hallmark
  • Urine reducing substances positive
  • Treatment: remove galactose/lactose (soy based formula)
exam_pearl: Cataract + liver disease + E. coli sepsis = galactosemia; lens dislocation instead points to homocystinuria.

stem: Cough , fevere developed SOB , on examination the child looks well basal crackles on rt lower chest auscaltation , stony dullness on percussion , T 38.5 ?
key_concept:
Percussion decides the chest finding.
  • Stony dullness = pleural effusion
  • Dull + bronchial breathing = consolidation (pneumonia)
  • Hyperresonant + absent breath sounds = pneumothorax
  • Dull + trachea shifted toward the side = collapse
  • A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to pleural effusion.
exam_pearl: Stony dullness means fluid in the pleural space; plain dullness with bronchial breathing means consolidation.

stem: Girl presented with bleeding per rectum , watery diarrhea , long standing nausea , epigastric pain?
key_concept:
Alarm features in pediatric GI complaints require investigation.
  • GI bleeding, anemia, weight loss / growth failure, nocturnal symptoms, persistent vomiting
  • Bloody diarrhea: infectious colitis, IBD
  • Painless large rectal bleed: Meckel (technetium scan)
  • Empirical PPI only for dyspepsia without alarm features
exam_pearl: Alarm features (bleeding, anemia, weight loss, growth failure) decide between investigating and treating empirically or reassuring.

stem: 7 years old girl presented with breast development and pubic hair , breast tanner 3 and pubic hair tanner 2 , normal fsh , lh , brain mri normal , high estradiol ?
why_right: A 7-year-old with breast Tanner 3 and pubic hair, high estradiol but gonadotropins that are not raised ("normal FSH, LH") and a "normal" brain MRI indicates estrogen production independent of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis: peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) precocious puberty, e.g. ovarian cyst or tumor, McCune-Albright, exogenous estrogen.
why_wrong_block: A. Central precocious puberty is driven by early activation of the HPG axis, so LH and FSH are raised into the pubertal range (especially after GnRH stimulation); non-raised gonadotropins with high estradiol argue against it.
key_concept:
Precocious puberty in girls: signs before age 8.
  • Central: high LH/FSH (stimulated LH rise), mostly idiopathic in girls; MRI brain; treat with GnRH agonist
  • Peripheral: high sex steroid with low/normal (suppressed) LH/FSH
  • Peripheral causes: ovarian cyst/tumor, McCune-Albright, adrenal, exogenous estrogen
  • Next step for peripheral: pelvic ultrasound
exam_pearl: High estradiol with gonadotropins that fail to rise = peripheral; read the LH/FSH, not the Tanner stage.

stem: Child 2 moth features (I forget ) protruded tongue , on cardiac exam significant murmur?
key_concept:
Syndrome first, then its signature heart lesion.
  • Down syndrome: AVSD (atrioventricular canal) most characteristic; VSD and ASD also occur
  • Turner syndrome: coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve
  • Congenital rubella: PDA
  • Williams syndrome: supravalvular aortic stenosis
  • Noonan syndrome: pulmonary valve stenosis
  • AVSD clue: superior QRS axis on ECG
exam_pearl: If the stem gives Down features, the answer is AVSD; VSD wins only when the question asks for the most common CHD in general.
