stem: Uncontrolled BA + greasy foul smell stool , next investigation?
why_right: Uncontrolled asthma together with greasy, foul smelling stool (steatorrhea) is cystic fibrosis until proven otherwise: chronic airway disease plus pancreatic insufficiency. The lead-in asks for the next investigation, and the first diagnostic test for suspected CF is the sweat chloride test. CFTR genetic testing confirms or is used when sweat results are borderline.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ct chest: shows bronchiectasis or structural lung damage once CF is known, but it cannot diagnose CF and does not explain the steatorrhea.
B. Brocho lavage: used to obtain airway cultures (for example Pseudomonas) or to evaluate infection in established lung disease; it is invasive and not a diagnostic test for CF.
key_concept:
Respiratory symptoms + malabsorption in a child = cystic fibrosis; first test is sweat chloride.
  • Diagnosis needs one clinical or context criterion plus one laboratory criterion
  • Lab criteria: raised sweat chloride on two occasions, or two CF-causing CFTR mutations
  • Other clues: failure to thrive, rectal prolapse, nasal polyps, meconium ileus
  • Sibling of an affected child: CFTR genetic testing
exam_pearl: Asthma that will not settle plus steatorrhea is not just bad asthma: think CF and order a sweat test.

stem: A 14-year-old girl presents with short stature, primary amenorrhea, and absent secondary sexual characteristics. Her karyotype is 45,X. What is the most appropriate treatment at this time?
why_right: The 45,X karyotype with short stature and absent puberty is Turner syndrome, where short stature is caused by SHOX haploinsufficiency, not GH deficiency. This recall's key is growth hormone because the classic teaching is to maximise height first while the epiphyses are open, since estrogen accelerates epiphyseal fusion and ends growth. Estrogen is then added to induce puberty.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oral contraceptive pills: not used to start puberty; induction uses low-dose estrogen increased gradually, and combined pills come later only for maintenance.
C. Estrogen therapy: needed in Turner syndrome to induce breasts and menses, so it is part of her care; the key ranks it after GH because early full-dose estrogen closes the growth plates and limits final height.
D. Gonadotropin replacement therapy: useless here because the problem is primary ovarian failure (streak gonads) with high FSH and LH; gonadotropins are for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
key_concept:
Turner syndrome treatment: height first, then puberty.
  • Diagnosis: karyotype 45,X (mosaicism possible)
  • Short stature: GH therapy while epiphyses are open
  • Ovarian failure: low-dose estrogen to induce puberty, progestin added later for cycles
  • Gonadotropins are not useful: FSH and LH are already high
  • Screen heart (coarctation, bicuspid valve) and kidneys (horseshoe kidney)
exam_pearl: In Turner syndrome the ovaries, not the pituitary, have failed: never give gonadotropins.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2517).

stem: Child(I think 2 month) came with his mother concern about chicken Pox infection after his exposure with child with chicken Pox several days. Child now asymptomatic what to do
why_right: A healthy 2-month-old exposed to chickenpox who is now asymptomatic needs no specific intervention, so the answer is to reassure the mother. Varicella immunoglobulin is reserved for high-risk exposures such as immunocompromised children, pregnant women, newborns whose mother develops varicella around delivery, and hospitalised preterm infants. The vaccine cannot be given before 12 months, and antibiotics have no role against a virus.
why_wrong_block:
B. give VZIG: right for high-risk contacts (immunocompromised child, newborn whose mother has varicella from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery, preterm infants in hospital); a healthy term 2-month-old is not in these groups.
C. give chicken box vaccine: live varicella vaccine is not licensed under 12 months, so it cannot be used for post-exposure prophylaxis in a 2-month-old.
D. give prophylaxis antibiotics: varicella is viral; antibiotics are only for secondary bacterial skin infection of established lesions.
key_concept:
Varicella post-exposure: decide by host risk and age.
  • Healthy infant under 12 months, asymptomatic: reassure and observe
  • Healthy non-immune child 12 months or older: vaccine within 3 to 5 days
  • Immunocompromised, pregnant, at-risk newborn or preterm: VZIG (IVIG if VZIG unavailable)
  • Antibiotics: never as prophylaxis
exam_pearl: Age decides it: under 12 months the vaccine is not an option, and a healthy term infant does not qualify for VZIG.

stem: 6 years came with his mother concern about chichen box infection after his exposure with child with chicken box 2 days. Child now asymptomatic what to do?
why_right: A healthy 6-year-old exposed to chickenpox 2 days ago who is asymptomatic is within the post-exposure window, so varicella vaccine is the answer (assuming he is not already immune). Given within 3 days, and up to 5 days, of exposure it can prevent or modify the illness, and it also protects against future exposures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observe for a few days: lets the post-exposure window close; observation alone fits a healthy infant too young for the vaccine, not a 6-year-old who can be vaccinated.
B. give IVIG: passive immunisation is for high-risk contacts (immunocompromised, pregnant, at-risk newborns) when VZIG is unavailable; a healthy child gets the vaccine instead.
D. I don't remember but irrelevant: a placeholder from the recall, not a management option.
key_concept:
Healthy non-immune child 12 months or older exposed to varicella: vaccinate within 3 to 5 days.
  • Vaccine within 3 days is most effective, up to 5 days acceptable
  • Immunocompromised or pregnant: VZIG, not live vaccine
  • Under 12 months and healthy: reassure
  • Already immune (prior disease or two doses): nothing needed
exam_pearl: Timing flips it: exposure within 5 days in a healthy child over 12 months = vaccine; a high-risk host = immunoglobulin.

stem: A 4-day-old infant is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for episodes of apnea. On examination, a continuous machinery-like murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border, and a wide pulse pressure is noted. A chest X-ray reveals bilateral pulmonary congestion ("wet lung"). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptC: Urgent surgical ligation of the ductus
why_right: A continuous machinery murmur at the left upper sternal border with a wide pulse pressure is a patent ductus arteriosus. In a 4-day-old in the NICU with apnea and pulmonary congestion, the ductus is hemodynamically significant, so the next step is pharmacological closure with a prostaglandin inhibitor (indomethacin or ibuprofen) to constrict the duct.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fluid restriction and diuretics: supportive measures that may accompany treatment, but they do not close the ductus and so do not address the cause of the congestion.
C. Urgent surgical ligation of the ductus: reserved for a significant PDA that fails medical closure or when NSAIDs are contraindicated (for example renal failure, active bleeding, NEC).
D. Prostaglandin E1 infusion: keeps the ductus OPEN; it is right for duct-dependent lesions such as TGA or critical coarctation, and here it would worsen the shunt.
key_concept:
Ductus drugs work in opposite directions.
  • Close a significant PDA: NSAID (indomethacin or ibuprofen); paracetamol is an alternative
  • NSAID fails or contraindicated: surgical ligation or catheter closure
  • Keep duct open in duct-dependent CHD: prostaglandin E1
  • PDA signs: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure
  • Congenital rubella: PDA
exam_pearl: Prostaglandin inhibitor closes the duct; prostaglandin E1 keeps it open: read the option wording carefully.

stem: A newborn infant weighing 2 kg (small for gestational age) is noted to have a depressed nasal bridge, hypertelorism, upward slanting palpebral fissures, and an elevated epicanthal fold. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: This recall's key is congenital infection screening (TORCH), presumably because the baby is small for gestational age (2 kg) and congenital infection is a recognised cause of growth restriction in a newborn. However, the face described (depressed nasal bridge, upward slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds) is the classic dysmorphism of Down syndrome, which is itself associated with low birth weight. The same question elsewhere in this file is keyed to chromosomal analysis, so treat this key as disputed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chromosomal analysis: the karyotype confirms a suspected chromosomal syndrome such as trisomy 21; it is the keyed answer for the duplicate of this question, but not for this recall.
B. Metabolic screening: routine newborn screening for inborn errors and congenital hypothyroidism; it is not targeted at a dysmorphic face or growth restriction.
D. Skeletal survey: right when skeletal dysplasia (short limbs, abnormal bones) or non-accidental injury is suspected; facial dysmorphism alone does not call for it.
key_concept:
Dysmorphic newborn: name the pattern, then pick the targeted test.
  • Upslanting fissures, epicanthal folds, flat nasal bridge: Down syndrome, confirm by karyotype
  • SGA with microcephaly, cataract, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, calcifications: TORCH screen
  • Short limbs or fractures: skeletal survey
  • Lethargy, poor feeding, jaundice: metabolic or thyroid screen
exam_pearl: SGA alone points to TORCH only when infection signs are present; a Down face points to karyotype.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-2390 → A. Chromosomal analysis. Confirm before the exam.

stem: A 37-week gestation baby on delivery has a heart rate below 100 beats per minute, blue extremities, a weak cry with grimace, and little flexion. What is the most accurate APGAR score?
why_right: Score each sign: heart rate below 100 = 1, blue extremities (pink body, acrocyanosis) = 1, grimace on stimulation = 1, weak cry (weak or irregular respiration) = 1, little flexion = 1. Every component scores 1, so the total is 5.
why_wrong_block:
A. 4: would require one component to score 0 (for example no heart rate, apnea or a limp baby); none is absent here.
C. 7: would need two components at the maximum of 2 (for example heart rate above 100 or a vigorous cry); every sign here is only partial.
D. 9: describes a nearly normal vigorous newborn with only acrocyanosis; this baby is bradycardic, weak and poorly flexed.
key_concept:
APGAR: 5 signs, each 0, 1 or 2.
  • Appearance: blue or pale 0, blue extremities 1, completely pink 2
  • Pulse: absent 0, below 100 = 1, 100 or more = 2
  • Grimace: no response 0, grimace 1, cry or active withdrawal 2
  • Activity: limp 0, some flexion 1, active movement 2
  • Respiration: absent 0, slow, irregular or weak cry 1, good strong cry 2
exam_pearl: Blue extremities score 1, not 0; only a fully blue or pale baby scores 0 for appearance.

stem: child i think 18month came for vaccinations, mother reported hx of chicken pox infection 2 months ago that was CONFIRMED CLINICALLY, rash subsided within a few days, mother also showed a picture of the rash and it was consistent with varicella. whats the best action regarding varicella vaccination
why_right: Varicella that was confirmed clinically by a health care provider, with a rash consistent with varicella, counts as evidence of immunity. Natural infection gives lifelong immunity, so the varicella vaccine is not needed and should not be given; the rest of the schedule continues as normal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Give ivig: passive immunisation is for high-risk, non-immune contacts after exposure; this child is well and already immune.
B. Give vaccine now: right for a non-immune child at 12 to 15 months or a child with an uncertain history; a provider-verified episode makes vaccination unnecessary.
C. Give vaccine at 2 years: there is no reason to delay or schedule a varicella dose in a child who is already immune.
key_concept:
Evidence of varicella immunity means no vaccine.
  • Immunity: age-appropriate vaccine doses, provider-diagnosed or verified varicella or zoster, laboratory evidence of immunity
  • Uncertain or parent-only history: vaccinate
  • Routine schedule: 2 doses; susceptible 13 years or older: 2 doses 4 weeks apart
  • Live vaccine: avoid in immunocompromised children
exam_pearl: A clinically confirmed episode equals immunity; it is the unverified history that gets vaccinated.

stem: Baby for 9m vaccination, which of the following would be considered a contraindication for vaccination.
why_right: Among these, only a moderate to severe acute illness (with or without fever) is a reason to defer the 9-month vaccines until the child recovers. Mild illness, unrelated drug allergies and current medication are common misconceptions and do not justify withholding vaccines.
why_wrong_block:
B. Penicillin allergy: vaccines do not contain penicillin, so it is not a contraindication; only anaphylaxis to a vaccine component or a prior dose is.
C. Pharmacological therapy: current antibiotics or most other drugs do not stop vaccination; the exceptions are immunosuppressive therapy (avoid live vaccines) and recent blood products (delay MMR and varicella).
key_concept:
True contraindications are few; most reasons to delay are myths.
  • Contraindication: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or a vaccine component
  • Defer: moderate or severe acute illness
  • Live vaccines: avoid in immunocompromise and pregnancy
  • Not contraindications: mild illness, low-grade fever, antibiotics, local reactions, unrelated allergies (penicillin)
exam_pearl: Moderate to severe illness is technically a precaution (defer), but it is the only listed option that changes the plan.

stem: A pic of rooting relfex, when will it disappear ?
why_right: The picture shows the rooting reflex: stroking the side of the mouth makes the infant turn toward and follow the stimulus. It is present from birth and disappears by about 4 months, as feeding becomes voluntary. Persistence beyond this age suggests a CNS problem.
why_wrong_block:
A. 2 months is too early for rooting; the asymmetrical tonic neck (fencing) reflex is the one that fades around 2 to 3 months.
C. 6 months is when the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes disappear, not rooting.
D. Rooting should be long gone by 8 months; this is around when the parachute reflex appears (a protective reflex that persists for life).
key_concept:
Primitive reflexes disappear in a predictable order; persistence or asymmetry is abnormal.
  • ATNR (fencing): about 2 to 3 months
  • Rooting and Galant: about 4 months
  • Moro and palmar grasp: about 6 months
  • Babinski (upgoing): until 12 to 18 months
  • Parachute: appears 8 to 10 months, never disappears
exam_pearl: Rooting = 4 months; do not confuse with Moro/grasp (6 months) or ATNR (2 to 3 months) when the picture is of the mouth.

stem: A 9 month baby, with 6 months bone age, GH is normal, IGF 1 is low
why_right: This recall mirrors the classic case of a 9-year-old with bone age 6 (the "months" in the stem are most likely a garbled "years"). A bone age delayed by 2 years or more points to a pathological cause, and a normal random GH with low IGF-1 shows inadequate GH action, since IGF-1 is produced in response to GH. Random GH is pulsatile and unreliable, so the low IGF-1 is the telling result, classified here as GH deficiency.
why_wrong_block:
A. Failure to thrive is weight faltering from poor intake or illness; it would show weight dropping across centiles first, not an isolated low IGF-1 with a delayed bone age.
B. Constitutional delay also has a delayed bone age, but IGF-1 is appropriate for bone age and growth velocity is normal, with a family history of late puberty; it would be right if labs were normal and a parent was a late bloomer.
key_concept:
Short stature: bone age plus IGF-1 sorts the causes.
  • Familial: bone age = chronological age, short parents, normal IGF-1
  • Constitutional delay: bone age delayed, normal velocity, family history of late puberty
  • GH deficiency: bone age delayed (often ≥2 years), low IGF-1, poor velocity
  • Confirm GH deficiency with GH stimulation testing
exam_pearl: A normal random GH does not exclude GH deficiency; low IGF-1 is the screening clue.

stem: A 14-year-old boy presents to the pediatric clinic complaining of recurrent crampy abdominal pain, persistent non-bloody diarrhea, and weight loss over the past 3 months. A colonoscopy is performed and reveals deep, longitudinal mucosal ulcerations alternating with areas of completely normal-appearing mucosa, alongside multiple aphthous ulcers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Chronic non-bloody diarrhea, crampy pain and weight loss in a teenager suggest IBD, and the colonoscopy decides the type. Deep longitudinal ulcers alternating with completely normal mucosa are skip lesions with a cobblestone pattern, and aphthous ulcers are early Crohn's lesions. This patchy, transmural pattern is Crohn's disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ulcerative colitis gives continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum upward with no skip areas, and usually bloody diarrhea with urgency; it would be right with bloody stools and diffuse friable mucosa.
C. Celiac disease is a small bowel disease seen on duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy) with positive tTG antibodies; it does not produce colonic ulceration.
D. Pseudomembranous colitis follows antibiotic use and shows yellow-white plaques (pseudomembranes) from C. difficile, with an acute course rather than 3 months of weight loss.
key_concept:
Crohn's vs UC is decided by distribution and depth.
  • Crohn's: mouth to anus, skip lesions, transmural, cobblestoning, granulomas, fistulas, strictures, often non-bloody
  • UC: rectum upward, continuous, mucosal only, bloody diarrhea, pseudopolyps
  • Aphthous ulcers and perianal disease favour Crohn's
exam_pearl: "Normal mucosa between ulcers" = skip lesions = Crohn's; continuous involvement from the rectum = UC.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric endocrine clinic by his mother due to concerns regarding his short stature. On physical examination, his height and weight are both tracking steadily along the 3rd percentile, and his systemic exam is otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation reveals a normal random TSH , FSH , but a low insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) level for his chronological age. A left wrist radiograph demonstrates a bone age of 6 years. Upon taking the family history, the physician notes that the mother short. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
why_right: Height on the 3rd centile with a bone age of 6 at age 9 is a 3-year delay, and a delay of 2 years or more points to a pathological cause. The low IGF-1 with otherwise normal pituitary tests (TSH, FSH) localises the problem to the GH axis. A short mother is a distractor: familial short stature does not lower IGF-1 or delay bone age.
why_wrong_block:
B. Familial short stature has a bone age equal to chronological age and normal IGF-1; it would be right if bone age were 9 with normal labs and short parents.
C. Nutritional failure to thrive affects weight before height and the child is usually thin with abnormal exam; here weight and height track together and the exam is normal.
D. Constitutional delay also shows a delayed bone age, but IGF-1 is normal for bone age and there is a family history of late puberty; the low IGF-1 points away from it.
key_concept:
Short child: check bone age, growth velocity and IGF-1.
  • Bone age normal + short parents: familial
  • Bone age delayed + normal IGF-1 + late-bloomer parent: constitutional
  • Bone age delayed ≥2 years + low IGF-1: GH deficiency (confirm with stimulation test, treat with GH)
exam_pearl: A short mother tempts "familial", but a delayed bone age plus low IGF-1 overrides family history.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Question repeated verbatim as a 'Q:' restatement below the answer (no separate answer).

stem: An unvaccinated child develops a high-grade fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a maculopapular rash that started behind the ears and spread downward to the trunk. On oral examination, small gray-white spots on an erythematous base (Koplik spots) are noted on the buccal mucosa. What is the most appropriate management?
OptB: Supportive and conservative care (fluids and antipyretics)
highlight_terms_source: behind the ears and spread downward
why_right: High fever with the 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik spots and a rash starting behind the ears and spreading downward is measles in an unvaccinated child. Measles is viral with no specific antiviral, so management is supportive: fluids, antipyretics and monitoring for complications. Vitamin A supplementation is also recommended for children with measles.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV acyclovir treats HSV and serious varicella infections; it has no activity against measles virus. It would be right for neonatal HSV or varicella in an immunocompromised child.
C. Antibiotics do not treat a viral illness; they are used only when a secondary bacterial complication such as pneumonia or otitis media develops.
key_concept:
Measles = clinical diagnosis, supportive treatment.
  • Prodrome: fever + cough, coryza, conjunctivitis
  • Koplik spots (pathognomonic) precede the rash
  • Rash: behind ears/face, spreads downward
  • Treatment: supportive + vitamin A; isolate
  • Complications: pneumonia (commonest cause of death), otitis media, encephalitis, SSPE years later
exam_pearl: Antivirals and antibiotics are traps in uncomplicated measles; add antibiotics only for a proven bacterial complication.

stem: Child with increasing jaundice, flapping tremor and decreased school performance. O/E stigmata of chronic liver disease are present. Which of the following is MOST APPROPRIATE management?
highlight_terms_source: increasing jaundice, flapping tremor and decreased school performance
why_wrong_block:
A. Liver biopsy (with hepatic copper measurement) can confirm Wilson disease, but it is an invasive diagnostic step and risky in a decompensated, likely coagulopathic child; it is not management.
B. A HIDA scan assesses biliary excretion (for example biliary atresia or acute cholecystitis); it does not address chronic liver disease with encephalopathy.
C. 24-hour urinary copper is a supportive diagnostic test for Wilson disease (with low ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings), but the question asks for management, not diagnosis.
key_concept:
Wilson disease: liver + brain + eyes in a young patient.
  • Liver: hepatitis, cirrhosis, acute liver failure
  • CNS: tremor, rigidity, behavioural change, falling school performance
  • Eyes: Kayser-Fleischer rings
  • Labs: low ceruloplasmin, high 24h urinary copper
  • Treatment: chelation (D-penicillamine), zinc for maintenance; liver transplant for fulminant or decompensated disease
exam_pearl: "Most appropriate management" asks for treatment; the three listed options are all investigations.
compiler_note:
⚠ Page lists only options A-C (liver biopsy, HIDA scan, 24h urinary copper) but prints 'Answer: D'; endorsed option does not exist on the page. Card mirrors this (answer 'D' with no D option).

stem: Pediatric pt with bronchiolitis treated conservatively with hydration and suction then develop fever 38 and loss of appetite and red pharynx. What will require further investigations?
why_right: Bronchiolitis and viral URTIs are managed supportively, and some fever with a red throat is part of the expected viral course. A fever that persists or rises instead of settling is the warning sign of a secondary bacterial infection (pneumonia, otitis media) or another diagnosis, so it is the finding that justifies further investigations such as a CBC or chest X-ray.
why_wrong_block: B. Pharyngeal erythema is a common, nonspecific finding in viral respiratory infections and by itself does not change management; it would matter only with features of bacterial pharyngitis (exudate, tender nodes, no cough).
key_concept:
Viral respiratory illness: investigate when the course deviates.
  • Expected: low-grade fever, coryza, cough, red throat, improvement over days
  • Red flags: persistent or high fever, worsening distress, hypoxia, poor feeding/dehydration, lethargy
  • Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis; routine tests are not needed
exam_pearl: Fever that persists beyond the expected viral course, not a red throat, prompts looking for a bacterial complication.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same question as the numbered recall 'Kid with fever, runny nose, for a few days. Now not improving, fever persisting and throat erythematous what makes u do further investigation A. persisting fever B. red throat' (Answer: A). The 'Q:' restatement answers A. Persistent high fever (answer line on p574).

stem: Concerned mom with her newborn ask about when is the time for screening for IDA:
why_right: Iron-deficiency anemia screening (Hb/CBC) is done for all infants at 9 to 12 months, because iron stores from birth are depleted by then and dietary intake is often inadequate. Of the options, 10 months is the only one inside this window. A repeat at 15 to 18 months is reserved for children with risk factors.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 2 months term infants still have iron stores from birth, so routine screening is not useful; physiological anemia of infancy is expected around this age.
B. At 4 months, stores are usually still adequate; 4 to 6 months is when iron supplementation or iron-rich complementary foods are started, especially in breastfed infants, not when screening is done.
D. 18 months is the optional repeat screen for at-risk children, not the universal first screen.
key_concept:
Well-baby screening timing.
  • IDA screen: 9 to 12 months (repeat 15 to 18 months if at risk)
  • Autism screen: about 18 to 24 months
  • Head circumference: up to 2 years
  • BMI: from 2 years
exam_pearl: Pick the age inside 9 to 12 months; 18 months is only the at-risk repeat.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler heading: Screening of IDA 9-12 months.

stem: Newborn delivered by vacuum, and had blood cross sutures (cephalohematoma), he had tachycardia and hypotension and Hb 7.5. What will you do?
why_right: A vacuum delivery with a scalp bleed that crosses the sutures is a subgaleal hemorrhage (the source calls it cephalohematoma, but a true cephalohematoma is limited by sutures and rarely causes shock). The subgaleal space can hold a large volume of blood, and tachycardia, hypotension and Hb 7.5 mean hemorrhagic shock. Management is volume replacement with IV fluids and blood transfusion.
why_wrong_block:
A. FFP corrects clotting factor deficiency and may be added if a coagulopathy is found, but it does not replace lost red cells; it is not the primary treatment for hemorrhagic shock with Hb 7.5.
B. "Immediate resuscitation" is too vague; option C states the specific resuscitation this baby needs (volume plus red cells for blood-loss shock).
key_concept:
Neonatal scalp swellings after instrumental delivery.
  • Caput succedaneum: scalp edema, crosses sutures, present at birth, resolves in about 48 hours
  • Cephalohematoma: subperiosteal, limited by sutures, appears gradually, risk of jaundice
  • Subgaleal hemorrhage: under the aponeurosis, crosses sutures, fluctuant, can cause hypovolemic shock
  • Shock + falling Hb: fluids and blood transfusion, check coagulation
exam_pearl: Crossing sutures + shock after vacuum = subgaleal hemorrhage; treat the blood loss with transfusion.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Blood crossing sutures actually suggests subgaleal hemorrhage (source labels it cephalohematoma).

stem: Child male with cryptorchidism, low lying epicanthal folds, nuchal skin, what is the ddx:
why_right: A boy with cryptorchidism, epicanthal folds (with low-set ears) and excess nuchal skin (webbed neck) has the Turner-like phenotype of Noonan syndrome. Unlike Turner, Noonan occurs in males with a normal karyotype; other features include short stature, hypertelorism and pulmonary valve stenosis.
why_wrong_block: A. Marfan syndrome causes a tall, thin habitus with arachnodactyly, ectopia lentis and aortic root dilation; it does not cause webbed neck or undescended testes.
key_concept:
Webbed neck: think Turner (girl, 45,X) or Noonan (either sex, normal karyotype).
  • Noonan: short stature, webbed neck, hypertelorism, low-set ears, ptosis, pulmonary stenosis, cryptorchidism
  • Turner: girl, short, webbed neck, shield chest, coarctation, primary amenorrhea
  • Prader-Willi: hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, undescended testes
  • Marfan: tall, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, aortic dilation
exam_pearl: Turner features in a boy = Noonan; right heart (pulmonary stenosis) in Noonan vs left heart (coarctation) in Turner.

stem: Child with Fecal soiling
why_right: In a child (beyond infancy) with fecal soiling, the usual cause is functional (idiopathic) constipation with overflow incontinence: retained hard stool stretches the rectum, sensation fades and loose stool leaks around the impaction. Soiling is a hallmark of functional constipation and points away from an organic obstruction.
why_wrong_block: B. Hirschsprung disease presents from the neonatal period with delayed meconium (beyond 24 to 48 hours), distension, bilious vomiting and an empty rectum with a squirt sign; soiling is rare because the aganglionic segment keeps the rectum empty.
key_concept:
Soiling in a child = functional constipation with overflow until proven otherwise.
  • Functional: onset after toddler years or toilet training, stool withholding, large stools, soiling, impacted stool on DRE.
  • Hirschsprung: symptoms since birth, delayed meconium, FTT, empty tight rectum, squirt sign.
  • Hirschsprung workup: contrast enema first, rectal biopsy confirms (absent ganglion cells).
  • Treatment of functional: disimpaction, osmotic laxative, toilet routine, diet.
exam_pearl: Soiling + stool in rectum = functional; constipation since birth + empty rectum = Hirschsprung.

stem: A 7-month-old child presents with vomiting and jaundice, but no hepatosplenomegaly. The child was previously healthy and tolerated breastfeeding well. Symptoms began after the introduction of fruits and fruit juices. Urine sediment test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Symptoms began after the introduction of fruits and fruit juices
why_right: A previously healthy, breastfed infant who becomes ill with vomiting and jaundice only after fruits and fruit juices are introduced has hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency). Fructose 1 phosphate accumulates, causing vomiting, hypoglycemia and liver injury, and fructose appears in the urine as a reducing substance (the positive urine test).
why_wrong_block:
B. Galactosemia presents in the first days of life once milk feeds start, because breast milk contains lactose; an infant who tolerated breastfeeding well for months does not have it.
C. Gluten sensitivity (celiac disease) follows introduction of wheat cereals and causes chronic diarrhea, distension and failure to thrive, not acute vomiting with jaundice after fruit.
key_concept:
Match the trigger food to the enzyme defect.
  • Fruit, juice, sucrose, honey: hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B).
  • Breast or formula milk from the first days: galactosemia (GALT); E. coli sepsis, cataracts.
  • Wheat cereals: celiac disease; diarrhea, FTT.
  • Positive urine reducing substances: fructose or galactose in urine.
  • Treatment of HFI: remove fructose, sucrose and sorbitol from the diet.
exam_pearl: Same picture starting with milk in the first week is galactosemia; starting at weaning with fruit is fructose intolerance.

stem: A child with a history of asthma presents for evaluation. His medical history is notable for atopic dermatitis. The patient has experienced recurrent episodes of wheezing and coughing, especially at night and with exposure to triggers. Which of the following provides objective evidence of asthma?
why_right: The question asks for objective evidence. Atopy, family history and night cough are all supportive history, but only spirometry gives an objective measure: reversible airflow obstruction, shown by an improvement in FEV1 of at least 12% after a bronchodilator, confirms asthma.
why_wrong_block:
A. Atopic dermatitis is part of the atopic march and raises the probability of asthma, but it is a history finding, not objective proof.
C. A family history of asthma is a risk factor that supports the diagnosis; it is subjective history and does not demonstrate airway disease in this child.
D. Nighttime cough is a typical symptom of asthma (and of poor control), but symptoms are subjective and shared with other causes of chronic cough.
key_concept:
Asthma diagnosis = typical symptoms + objective variable airflow obstruction.
  • Spirometry: FEV1/FVC reduced (obstructive).
  • Reversibility: FEV1 or FVC rise ≥12% after bronchodilator.
  • Normal spirometry but high suspicion: methacholine challenge (FEV1 fall ≥20% = positive).
  • Peak flow variability is an alternative objective test.
  • History (atopy, family history, night symptoms) supports but never proves.
exam_pearl: "Objective evidence" in the lead in means a test result, not a history item.

stem: 18 months old boy, came to clinic for review. The child is always hungry, drinks 1 litter of milk daily and eats dirt. Poor solid food intake. On exam He is underweight & has pale conjunctiva. Which the most appropriate investigation?
why_right: An 18 month old drinking 1 litre of milk daily with poor solid intake, pica (eating dirt), underweight and pale conjunctiva has iron deficiency anemia until proven otherwise. The first investigation is a CBC with blood smear: it confirms anemia, shows microcytic hypochromic indices and the smear features, and directs any further iron studies.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lead screening is reasonable in a child with pica, and lead toxicity can coexist with iron deficiency, but the pallor and milk excess call first for confirming and characterising the anemia.
C. Ophthalmology consultation has no role; pale conjunctiva is a sign of anemia, not an eye disease.
D. Ferritin confirms low iron stores and is a useful second step, but on its own it does not show whether anemia is present or its severity; the CBC comes first.
key_concept:
Toddler + excess cow's milk + pica + pallor = iron deficiency anemia.
  • Cow's milk is iron poor, displaces solid food and can cause occult GI blood loss in children under 2.
  • First test: CBC with smear (low Hb, low MCV, hypochromia, often high platelets).
  • Then iron studies: low ferritin, high TIBC.
  • Pica: think iron deficiency and lead exposure.
  • Treatment: limit milk, oral ferrous sulfate, recheck response.
exam_pearl: Ferritin confirms the cause, but the CBC confirms the anemia; the lead in "most appropriate investigation" here wants the CBC first.

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with history of increasing eye puffiness for 1 week especially in the morning. He has had flu-like illness 2 week ago. On examination, he looks well, not in distress and no lower limb edema. Eye, chest and abdomen exams are normal (see lab results). Blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, Heart rate 88 /min, Respiratory rate 18 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 95 %. Total Proteins 35 (56-80 g/L), Albumin 16 (36-52 g/L), Protein +4 (Absent). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 5 year old with morning periorbital puffiness, normal blood pressure, albumin 16 g/L, low total protein and proteinuria 4+ has nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and edema. In this age group the cause is usually minimal change disease, often following a viral illness.
why_wrong_block:
A. Nephritic syndrome (e.g. post-infectious GN) gives hematuria, hypertension, oliguria and only mild proteinuria; here BP is 100/70 and the albumin is profoundly low, which fits nephrotic.
C. Hereditary angioedema causes episodic non-pitting swelling of face, lips or airway with normal albumin and no proteinuria.
D. Protein losing enteropathy also causes hypoalbuminemia and edema, but protein is lost in the gut, so the urine is free of protein; 4+ proteinuria points to the kidney.
key_concept:
Nephrotic = proteinuria + hypoalbuminemia + edema (+ hyperlipidemia).
  • Proteinuria in nephrotic range (>3.5 g/day adult; 3+ to 4+ dipstick).
  • Periorbital edema worst in the morning.
  • Nephritic: hematuria, RBC casts, hypertension, oliguria.
  • Child 2 to 6 years: minimal change disease; steroids first, biopsy not routinely needed.
  • Low albumin without proteinuria: think gut loss or liver.
exam_pearl: A preceding viral illness is a trap toward post-infectious nephritis; normal BP and massive proteinuria keep it nephrotic.

stem: Father has SC trait with 2 brothers who have SCD. Married a woman her family without SCD and the woman didn't test yet. What is the risk for baby?
OptD: Low risk and nil if mother test negative
why_right: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive: a child is affected only if both parents pass a sickle gene. The father is a carrier, and the mother comes from a family without SCD and is untested, so the baby's risk of disease is low, and becomes nil if her hemoglobin electrophoresis is normal (the child could at most be a carrier). The correct step is to test the mother.
why_wrong_block:
A. High risk applies when both partners are known carriers (1 in 4 risk of SCD per pregnancy); only the father is known to carry the gene here.
B. No risk cannot be stated until the mother is tested; an untested partner could still be a silent carrier.
C. Advising against having children is not appropriate counselling, and even for two carriers the role is to inform options, not to forbid pregnancy.
key_concept:
Autosomal recessive counselling depends on BOTH partners' carrier status.
  • Carrier × non carrier: 0% disease, 50% carriers.
  • Carrier × carrier: 25% disease, 50% carriers, 25% unaffected.
  • Untested partner: test with hemoglobin electrophoresis before counselling a risk.
  • Affected relatives (his brothers) do not change the risk if the partner is negative.
exam_pearl: Father's affected brothers are a distractor; the risk hinges on the mother's test.

stem: A 6-years old with noticed progressive jaundice and mild tremors with decreased school performance. On examination there is stigmata of few chronic liver injuries. See labs. Hb 7, Retics 6, Direct bilirubin 20, Total bilirubin 25. What is the gold standard for diagnosis?
why_right: A 6 year old with progressive jaundice, tremor, declining school performance, signs of chronic liver disease and hemolytic anemia (Hb 7, reticulocytes 6) has Wilson disease. The lead in asks for the gold standard: liver biopsy with quantification of hepatic copper content is the definitive diagnostic test, since serum ceruloplasmin and urinary copper can be equivocal.
why_wrong_block:
B. A HIDA scan assesses biliary excretion (biliary atresia, cholecystitis) and does not diagnose a copper storage disease.
C. Bone marrow aspiration is for suspected leukemia or marrow failure; the high reticulocyte count here shows the marrow is responding to hemolysis.
D. 24 hour urine copper is the most practical screening and supportive test for Wilson disease, but it is not the gold standard; that is hepatic copper on liver biopsy.
key_concept:
Wilson disease: liver + neuro/psychiatric + Coombs negative hemolysis in a child or young adult.
  • Screening: low ceruloplasmin, high 24 h urine copper, slit lamp for Kayser Fleischer rings.
  • Gold standard: liver biopsy with hepatic copper quantification.
  • Genetic testing (ATP7B) confirms in family screening.
  • Treatment: chelation (penicillamine or trientine), zinc for maintenance.
exam_pearl: "Gold standard" = liver biopsy; "most appropriate investigation" (sister card) = 24 h urine copper.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-2352 → D. 24h urine copper excretion. Confirm before the exam.

stem: A 6-years old with noticed progressive jaundice and mild tremors with decreased school performance. On examination there is stigmata of few chronic liver injuries. See labs. Hb 7, Retics 6, Direct bilirubin 20, Total bilirubin 25. What is the Most appropriate Investigation?
why_right: Progressive jaundice, tremor, falling school performance, chronic liver stigmata and hemolysis (Hb 7, reticulocytes 6) in a 6 year old point to Wilson disease. The lead in asks for the most appropriate investigation, meaning the practical noninvasive test: 24 hour urinary copper excretion is high in Wilson disease and is used with serum ceruloplasmin and slit lamp exam to make the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Liver biopsy with hepatic copper is the gold standard, but it is invasive and reserved for when noninvasive tests are inconclusive; it is not the first appropriate test.
B. A HIDA scan evaluates biliary drainage (biliary atresia, cholecystitis) and has no role in copper storage disease.
C. Bone marrow aspiration is for leukemia or marrow failure; the raised reticulocytes show an active marrow responding to hemolysis.
key_concept:
Wilson disease workup ladder.
  • First: serum ceruloplasmin (low), 24 h urine copper (high), slit lamp for Kayser Fleischer rings.
  • Equivocal: liver biopsy with hepatic copper (gold standard).
  • Genetics: ATP7B mutation analysis.
  • Clues: hepatitis or cirrhosis + tremor or behaviour change + Coombs negative hemolysis.
exam_pearl: Same stem, different lead in: "gold standard" flips the answer to liver biopsy.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-2351 → A. Liver biopsy. Confirm before the exam.

stem: A 2-year-old girl brought to Primary Clinic because the mother noticed she is pale. She had history of drinking 3 glasses of cow's milk daily, very picky eater and refusing to eat meat. The mother gave history of similar presentation on 2 of her brother (see lab results). RBC 3 (4.8-7.1 x 10^12/L Newborn; 4.6-4.8 x 10^12/L Child), Hb 4 (165-195 g/L Newborn; 112-165 g/L Child), MCH 18 (28-33 pg/cell), MCV 62 (80-95 fl), Reticulocyte 3 (0.2-1.2 %), Platelets count 480 (150-400 x 10^9/L), Ferritin 9 (20-200 g/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: drinking 3 glasses of cow's milk daily
why_right: This recall is keyed to sickle cell disease. The source's reasoning rests on the similar presentation in 2 brothers, a familial pattern that points to an inherited hemoglobinopathy (autosomal recessive, so siblings share it), and on reticulocytes 3%, above the printed range, suggesting increased red cell turnover. A suspected hemoglobinopathy in a pale child is confirmed by hemoglobin electrophoresis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Alpha thalassemia trait gives only a mild microcytic anemia with a normal or high RBC count and normal ferritin; Hb this low with ferritin 9 does not fit a trait.
C. Iron deficiency fits the cow's milk excess, refusal of meat, MCV 62, ferritin 9 and platelets 480, but this recall's key gives more weight to the two affected brothers, a familial pattern that a dietary cause does not explain.
D. Anemia of chronic disease needs an underlying chronic inflammatory illness, none is described, and ferritin is normal or raised rather than 9.
key_concept:
Pale child with microcytic indices: sort nutrition, inheritance and inflammation.
  • Iron deficiency: excess cow's milk, poor meat intake, low ferritin, reactive thrombocytosis.
  • Sickle cell disease: chronic hemolytic anemia, raised reticulocytes, affected siblings (autosomal recessive).
  • Thalassemia trait: microcytosis with normal ferritin and high RBC count.
  • Anemia of chronic disease: chronic illness, normal or high ferritin.
  • Suspected hemoglobinopathy: confirm with hemoglobin electrophoresis.
exam_pearl: Affected siblings are the clue this key rests on; check the answer concern on this card before the exam.
compiler_note:
⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-2354 → C. Iron deficiency anemia. Confirm before the exam.
Compiler note: Page prints Answer: A for this version; the near identical recalls 2354 and 2355 are answered C (Iron deficiency anemia).

stem: A 2-year-old girl brought to Primary Clinic because the mother noticed she is pale. History of drinking 3 pints of cow's milk daily and is a very picky eater. The mother gave history of similar presentation on 2 of her brother (see lab results). RBC 3 (4.8-7.1 x 10^12/L Newborn; 4.6-4.8 x 10^12/L Child), Hb 4 (165-195 g/L Newborn; 112-165 g/L Child), MCH 18 (28-33 pg/cell), MCV 62 (80-95 fl), Reticulocyte 3 (0.2-1.2 %), Platelets count 480 (150-400 x 10^9/L), Ferritin 9 (20-200 ug/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: drinking 3 pints of cow's milk daily
why_right: A 2 year old drinking 3 pints of cow's milk daily and eating poorly, with MCV 62, MCH 18, ferritin 9 and platelets 480, has iron deficiency anemia. Cow's milk is iron poor, displaces iron rich food and can cause occult intestinal blood loss in toddlers; low ferritin is diagnostic and reactive thrombocytosis is typical.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sickle cell disease causes a normocytic hemolytic anemia with normal or high ferritin; the affected brothers are a distractor, and the diagnosis would need Hb electrophoresis, not a dietary history.
B. Alpha thalassemia trait is microcytic but gives only mild anemia with a relatively high RBC count and normal or high ferritin; ferritin 9 and Hb this low point to iron deficiency instead.
D. Anemia of chronic disease requires a chronic inflammatory illness and has normal or raised ferritin, usually with normocytic indices.
key_concept:
Low Hb + low MCV + low ferritin (+ high TIBC, high platelets) = iron deficiency anemia.
  • Risk: under 2 years with excess cow's milk, picky eating, no meat.
  • Thalassemia trait: microcytosis with normal ferritin and high RBC count.
  • Anemia of chronic disease: normal or high ferritin.
  • Treatment: limit milk, oral ferrous sulfate, recheck response.
exam_pearl: Family history of anemia in siblings is a trap toward hemoglobinopathy; ferritin decides.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-2353 → A. Sickle cell disease. Confirm before the exam.

stem: A 2-Year-Old Girl Brought To Primary Clinic Because The Mother Noticed She Is Pale. She Had History Of Drinking excessive amounts Of Milk and refuse to eat and solid food, Very Picky Eater And Refusing To Eat Meat. The Mother Gave History Of Similar Presentation On 2 Of Her Brother. Lab Results: RBC: 3, Hb: 4, MCH: 18, MCV: 62, Reticulocyte: 3%, Platelets Count: 480, Ferritin: 9. Which Of The Following Is The Most Likely Diagnosis?
why_right: A toddler with excessive milk intake, refusal of solids and refusing meat has an iron poor diet, and cow's milk in young children also causes occult gut blood loss and reduces iron absorption. The labs confirm it: microcytosis (MCV 62), low MCH, ferritin 9 (low ferritin is diagnostic of iron deficiency) and platelets 480 (reactive thrombocytosis). The low RBC count also fits IDA, since MCV/RBC (62/3) is well above 13.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sickle cell disease is a normocytic hemolytic anemia with clearly raised reticulocytes, jaundice and normal or high ferritin; it does not give MCV 62 with ferritin 9. The brothers' history is a distractor toward hemoglobinopathy.
B. Alpha thalassemia trait is microcytic but the anemia is mild, the RBC count is high and ferritin is normal; it would fit a well child with MCV low but Hb near normal and normal iron studies.
D. Anemia of chronic disease needs an underlying chronic inflammatory illness and has normal or high ferritin; it is right when ferritin is normal or raised with low TIBC in a chronically ill child.
key_concept:
Microcytic anemia: ferritin decides first.
  • Low ferritin, high TIBC, high platelets = iron deficiency
  • Normal/high ferritin, high RBC, mild anemia = thalassemia trait
  • Normal/high ferritin, low TIBC, chronic illness = anemia of chronic disease
  • Mentzer (MCV/RBC): >13 favours IDA, <13 favours thalassemia
  • Toddler on lots of cow's milk = classic IDA risk
exam_pearl: Family history of anemia is the trap; ferritin 9 with a milk heavy, meat free diet still means iron deficiency.

stem: An 8-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Room by her mother after ingestion of large amount of acetaminophen tablets. According to the mother, she ingested full 2 packs, containing 20 tablets. 1 day ago after she had fight with her. On examination, she has right upper quadrant abdominal pain, with nausea and vomiting. Blood pressure 95/50 mmHg, Heart rate 135 /min, Respiratory rate 25 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 95 %. Which phase of acetaminophen toxicity she is at?
why_right: The ingestion was 1 day ago and she now has right upper quadrant abdominal pain, which reflects hepatic injury. Phase 2 (roughly 24 to 72 hours) is when the early GI upset settles but RUQ pain and liver tenderness appear with rising transaminases. She has no jaundice, encephalopathy or anuria, so she has not reached phase 3.
why_wrong_block:
A. Phase 1 is the first 24 hours: only anorexia, nausea, vomiting and malaise with normal labs; RUQ pain marks the move into phase 2.
C. Phase 3 (about days 3 to 4) is fulminant hepatic failure: jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, anuria; none is described here.
D. Phase 4 (from about day 4 to 2 weeks) is either recovery with normalising labs or progression to multiorgan failure and death.
key_concept:
Paracetamol toxicity phases by time and liver signs.
  • Phase 1 (0 to 24 h): nausea, vomiting, malaise, normal labs
  • Phase 2 (24 to 72 h): RUQ pain, liver tenderness, rising AST/ALT
  • Phase 3 (72 to 96 h): jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, renal failure
  • Phase 4 (about day 4 to 2 weeks): recovery or death
  • Symptomatic or raised LFTs at any phase: give N acetylcysteine
exam_pearl: RUQ pain or tenderness = phase 2; add jaundice or confusion and it becomes phase 3.

stem: 10 Y/O Child with cystic fibrosis, and the parent is asking what the proper counseling for this patient is. Which of the following is most appropriate?
OptC: No Need to test until 18 years old
OptD: Random blood glucose every six months
why_right: Cystic fibrosis related diabetes develops from progressive pancreatic damage and is often silent early, with fasting glucose staying normal until late. Guidelines therefore recommend an annual oral glucose tolerance test starting at age 10 in all people with CF, which matches this 10 year old. The OGTT detects post load hyperglycemia that fasting or random glucose misses.
why_wrong_block:
B. Fasting glucose is insensitive in CF because early CF related diabetes shows post prandial hyperglycemia with a normal fasting value; it is the usual screen in type 2 diabetes risk groups, not CF.
C. Waiting until 18 misses years of undetected diabetes; screening begins at age 10.
D. Random glucose is not a screening test; it only diagnoses diabetes when ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms.
key_concept:
CF related diabetes screening = annual OGTT from age 10.
  • Cause: pancreatic islet destruction (insulin deficiency)
  • Early phase: normal fasting glucose, high 2 hour value
  • HbA1c alone is not reliable for screening in CF
  • Treatment of CF related diabetes: insulin
exam_pearl: In CF the fasting glucose looks normal long after diabetes has started, so only the OGTT catches it.

stem: A 2-year-old girl with a high, relapsing fever of 9-day duration associated with marked irritability. a non-purulent conjunctivitis, red cracked lips, swollen and erythematous hands and feet, and a maculopapular erythematous rash on the trunk and extremities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: swollen and erythematous hands and feet
why_right: Fever for 9 days (more than 5) plus four principal features, non-purulent conjunctivitis, red cracked lips, swollen erythematous hands and feet and a polymorphous rash, meets the criteria for Kawasaki disease. Marked irritability out of proportion to the fever is also typical. The next steps are echocardiography for coronary aneurysms and IVIG with aspirin.
why_wrong_block:
A. EBV mononucleosis gives exudative pharyngitis, generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes, not cracked lips with swollen red hands and feet.
C. Rubella is mild with low grade fever, a cephalocaudal rash and postauricular or suboccipital nodes lasting about 3 days, not 9 days of high fever.
D. Measles has cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots and a cephalocaudal rash; it does not cause extremity swelling or cracked lips.
key_concept:
Kawasaki = fever ≥5 days + 4 of 5 features (CRASH).
  • Conjunctivitis: bilateral, non-purulent
  • Rash: polymorphous
  • Adenopathy: cervical, usually single node
  • Strawberry tongue / red cracked lips
  • Hands and feet: edema, erythema, later desquamation
  • Investigate with echo; treat with IVIG plus aspirin
exam_pearl: Non-purulent conjunctivitis plus hand and foot swelling separates Kawasaki from measles.
